objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-what-is-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-what-is-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Question: What Is Error?
When we talk about error in epidemiology, we are generally talking about the difference between the true underlying population value of interest and our measure (or estimate) of that value.
A. True
B. False

True. Error is simply the difference between the truth and our estimate of the truth.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-what-is-truth
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-what-is-truth
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Big Picture: What Is Truth?
text:
The Big Picture: What Is Truth?



Another way to say this is that the truth is equal to our measure of the truth minus the error in our measure.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-truth-by-another-name
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-truth-by-another-name
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Big Picture: Truth by Another Name
text:
The Big Picture: Truth by Another Name



Another term that we will use to refer to the true quantity we aspire to measure in our target population is estimand. Likewise, another term that we will use to refer to the quantity that actually resulted from our data collection and analysis is estimate.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-truth-from-another-perspective
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-truth-from-another-perspective
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Big Picture: Truth from Another Perspective
text:
The Big Picture: Truth from Another Perspective



Graphically, that might look something like this. When we conduct a study in epidemiology, we end up with estimates. Those estimates are a result of the true underlying population value – the truth – and the error in our measures.
In this sense, error can simply be taken to mean the literal difference between our estimate of the truth and the actual truth. It doesn’t have to be any more complicated than that. Later, our description of errors will get more detailed, and our discussion of the effects of errors will get more specific, but we will still be having a more detailed and specific discussion about this basic idea – the difference between our estimate and the truth.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#quick-terminology-review
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#quick-terminology-review
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Quick Terminology Review
Match each term to its definition.


Terms

Estimand
Estimator
Estimate
Error


Definitions
A. The quantity that actually resulted from our data collection and analysis.
B. The difference between the estimate and the estimand.
C. The true quantity we aspire to measure in our target population.
D. The analysis technique or algorithm used to produce the estimate from our data.



Answers: 1–C (estimand); 2–D (estimator); 3–A (estimate); 4–B (error).

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-accuracy
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-accuracy
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
The Big Picture: Accuracy



And the accuracy of our estimate is a measure of how close it is to the truth.

Or how much error we have.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-estimate-without-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-estimate-without-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Big Picture: Estimate without Error
text:
The Big Picture: Estimate without Error



Why does this matter? It matters because our goal is to know the truth or at least to know something “close enough” to the truth for our purposes. In theory, if we can eliminate error or at least quantify and correct for it, then we can know the truth.
At this point, you may be thinking to yourself, “easier said than done,” and we would tend to agree. Completely removing, or even perfectly quantifying, the error in our estimates is typically difficult work and is often accompanied by our old friend uncertainty. However, and we will keep coming back to this, we can often do a “good enough” job for our results to be useful for our purposes.
As a next step in thinking about how to eliminate and/or quantify error, it can be useful to learn more about the various ways we get error in our measurements in the first place.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#quick-review-types-of-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#quick-review-types-of-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Quick Review: Types of Error
The two highest-level (most general) categories of error are typically considered to be…
A. Bias and confounding
B. Random and systematic
C. Differential and non-differential
D. Ignorable and non-ignorable


Correct answer: B. Random and systematic.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-types-of-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-big-picture-types-of-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Big Picture: Types of Error
text:
The Big Picture: Types of Error



Traditionally, error is first categorized as random or systematic.

We’ve already talked a lot about systematic error. What was another name we used for systematic error?

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-random-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-random-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
What is random error?



Well, we already know what error is, but what is random error? You might say that it is error that occurs at random, but what does that mean? What does it mean when we say that something is random?
When we use random in everyday speech, we typically mean that something happens for no reason – there is an effect without a cause.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#thought-experiment-chance-and-predictions
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#thought-experiment-chance-and-predictions
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Thought Experiment: Chance and Predictions
If we just had enough information about causes and effects, then we could perfectly predict every outcome.
A. True
B. False
C. Not sure


Modern Epidemiology, chapter 15, discusses the competing views about randomness.
One school of thought is that chance (lack of a cause?) plays a central role in virtually all processes.
The other is that chance is just an umbrella term for causes we don’t fully understand. In other words, there is a reason for everything that happens whether we know it or not.

Luckily, in epidemiology, random error (chance) can be defined a little bit more precisely. That’s what we will discuss next.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#how-stressed-are-students
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#how-stressed-are-students
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
How Stressed Are Students?
A campus wellness team wants to estimate the mean stress score among all undergraduates this semester.

Population: All undergraduates this semester.
Parameter: Their population mean StressScore.
Sample: 12 randomly selected students.

Should we expect the mean stress score from these 12 students to be the same as the mean for all undergraduates?


Ask students whether they expect the sample mean to equal the population mean, and have them explain their predictions.
We’ve already discussed bias and confounding. Today, we will discuss sampling variability.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#explore-the-population-in-excel
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#explore-the-population-in-excel
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Explore the Population in Excel
Open the Excel sampling demonstration and select the Population worksheet.

Each row represents one student in a simulated population of 10,000 students.
These are computer-generated example StressScores, not actual student records.
Calculate the mean of all 10,000 scores: =AVERAGE(B7:B10006).


Population mean: 20.99 points.


Instructions

Orient students to the Population Sheet.
Select E3 and type =AVERAGE(B7:B10006) in the formula bar.

Explain that averaging all 10,000 scores gives the population mean: 20.99 points.

We only know this value because we created the entire simulated population. In most real-world scenarios, we won’t have this information.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#explore-one-sample-in-excel
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#explore-one-sample-in-excel
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Explore One Sample in Excel
Select the Samples worksheet and locate Sample 1.

This random sample contains 12 students from the simulated population.
Find their student IDs and StressScores.
Calculate the mean of their 12 scores.


Sample mean: 21.98 points.


Instructions

Switch to Samples. Explain that each row represents a different prepared random sample.

For Sample 1 in row 8, show the 12 student IDs in AB8:AM8 and their scores in O8:Z8. These students were selected from the population just shown.

Select C8 and show =AVERAGE(O8:Z8) in the formula bar. This averages only the 12 scores in Sample 1, giving a sample mean of 21.98 points.

Ask: “Is this the same as 20.99? Is our sample mean above or below the population mean?”

In most real-world scenarios, we will only have information from our sample.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#one-population-one-sample
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#one-population-one-sample
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
One Population, One Sample
The sample mean is an estimate of the population mean.



Here, we plotted our population mean (20.987924) and our sample mean (21.9766667).

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-same-population-another-sample
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-same-population-another-sample
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
The Same Population, Another Sample
Sample 2 contains another random selection of 12 students from the same population.

The population stays the same. The sample estimate changes.


And we could do the same thing with sample 2.

Notice that the mean of sample 2 is once again different from the population mean, but it is also different from the mean of sample 1.

The population mean hasn’t changed, but our sample, and therefore our estimate of the population mean, has changed.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#in-a-real-study-the-population-mean-is-unknown
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#in-a-real-study-the-population-mean-is-unknown
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: In a Real Study, the Population Mean Is Unknown
text:
In a Real Study, the Population Mean Is Unknown


What We Observe
Sample 1’s mean StressScore:
21.98 points

What We Want to Know
The mean among all undergraduates:
?

How much might an estimate vary just because we sampled different students?


So, to drive this point home:

We usually sample because measuring the entire population is impractical.

Knowing the sample mean does not reveal its exact distance from the unknown population mean.

But that’s exactly what we want to know. The distance (the error) so that we can eliminate it and know the truth.

Unfortunately, we can rarely ascertain that answer for one sample, but we can quantify the variability of estimates across repeated samples.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#sampling-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#sampling-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Sampling Error
Sampling error=Sample mean−Population mean
\text{Sampling error} = \text{Sample mean} - \text{Population mean}




Sample
Sample Mean
Population Mean
Sampling Error




1
21.98
20.99
+0.99


2
20.16
20.99
−0.83



A positive error is an overestimate. A negative error is an underestimate.


Here, error means the difference between an estimate and the population value.

Tie this to measurement error and standard deviations.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#repeated-samples-different-means
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#repeated-samples-different-means
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Repeated Samples, Different Means
These are the first 10 samples in the Excel sampling demonstration. Each has 12 students.

The dashed line marks the population mean of 20.99.


For example, our true estimand of interest is the mean stress score.

We do 10 studies, each of which produces an estimate of the mean stress score.

In this hypothetical scenario, we know that the true mean stress score is 20.99. However, we can see here that none of the estimates produced by our 10 studies were exactly equal to 20.99. Therefore, there is error in each of the studies.

How much?

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-same-samples-shown-as-errors
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#the-same-samples-shown-as-errors
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: The Same Samples, Shown as Errors
text:
The Same Samples, Shown as Errors

Subtract the population mean from each sample mean. The dashed line now marks zero error.


Well, if we change the y-axis from the mean stress score to the error in the estimate of the true mean stress score (sampling error), we can see the amount of error in each estimate.

For example, study number one overestimates the population mean by about one point. 21.98 − 20.99 = +0.99 points.

Ask: What about study 2?

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#do-the-errors-cancel-out
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#do-the-errors-cancel-out
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Do the Errors Cancel Out?

For these 10 samples: sum of errors ≈ +1.06 points; average error ≈ +0.106 points.
The errors in a particular set of samples need not sum to zero.


And if we average the errors across repeated samples, they average toward zero in the long run.
Positive and negative errors offset one another, but this batch still has a small positive average error. A nonzero average in ten samples does not establish that the estimator is biased.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#average-of-the-sample-means
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#average-of-the-sample-means
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Average of the Sample Means

Average of the 10 sample means ≈ 21.09 points. Population mean ≈ 20.99 points.
An unbiased estimator has zero expected error across repeated samples.


And if we change the y-axis back to the original scale, we can see that the average of the estimates is 21.09.

The average sample mean is about 0.106 points above the population mean, matching the average error on the previous slide.
Under simple random sampling, the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean. Across all possible samples of the same size, its expected value equals the population mean.

Over many independent repetitions, the average sample mean tends toward the population mean, and the average error tends toward zero. This does not mean each additional sample brings the average closer or that any finite batch must match exactly.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#how-much-might-our-estimate-vary
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#how-much-might-our-estimate-vary
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: How Much Might Our Estimate Vary?
text:
How Much Might Our Estimate Vary?
In our demonstration, we knew the population mean, so we could calculate each sample’s error.
In a real study, we usually have one sample and an unknown population mean.
We cannot calculate our sample’s exact error, but we can estimate how much sample means would vary across repeated samples.

The standard error summarizes that variability.
A confidence interval uses it to express uncertainty around our estimate.



So far, we’ve been able to compare every sample mean with the truth. In a real study, we usually don’t have that luxury. We have our sample, but we don’t know the population mean—that’s what we’re trying to estimate.
We can’t tell exactly how far off our estimate is. But we can use the variation in our sample to estimate how much sample means would vary if we repeated the sampling process. That brings us to standard errors and confidence intervals.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#standard-deviation-and-standard-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#standard-deviation-and-standard-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Standard Deviation and Standard Error
For the separate Prep 4 worked sample of 12 students:



Measure
What Varies?
StressScore Example




Standard deviation
Individual scores within the sample
3.64 points


Standard error
Sample means across repeated samples
1.05 points



For a sample mean, estimate the standard error as sample SD ÷ √n.


Compare SD and SE, then discuss sample size and precision. These numbers come from the Prep 4 workbook, not Sample 1 of the sampling demonstration.
The sample SD describes the spread of individual scores. The SE estimates the SD of the sampling distribution of the mean.
Here, 3.64 ÷ √12 is about 1.05. Use full precision when calculating interval endpoints.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-a-confidence-interval
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-a-confidence-interval
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
What Is a Confidence Interval?
Our sample mean is 21 points. It estimates the population mean, but another sample would give us a different estimate.
A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the population mean, based on our sample and the method’s assumptions.

It expresses uncertainty due to random sampling.
Its width tells us about the estimate’s precision: a narrower interval gives a more precise estimate.
A 95% confidence level means that, over many repeated samples, about 95% of intervals constructed using this method would contain the true population mean.



In our demonstration, we knew the population mean. In a real study, we don’t. We use the sample to construct an interval, but we cannot check whether that particular interval captures the truth.
The 21-point sample mean comes from the separate Prep 4 worked sample of 12 students introduced on the previous slide.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-the-margin-of-error
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-is-the-margin-of-error
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: What Is the Margin of Error?
text:
What Is the Margin of Error?
For a population mean, we will construct a confidence interval by adding and subtracting a margin of error from the sample mean.
Sample mean±Margin of error
\text{Sample mean} \pm \text{Margin of error}

The margin of error is the distance from the sample mean to either endpoint.
For our worked example:
21.00±2.31=18.69 to 23.31
21.00 \pm 2.31 = 18.69 \text{ to } 23.31

A larger margin of error produces a wider confidence interval.


The margin of error is not the actual distance between our sample mean and the population mean. We still don’t know that distance.
Adding and subtracting the same margin gives us a symmetric interval in this example. Not all confidence intervals are symmetric around their estimates.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#calculating-a-confidence-interval-for-a-population-mean
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#calculating-a-confidence-interval-for-a-population-mean
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: Calculating a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
text:
Calculating a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
The margin of error is the standard error multiplied by a critical value. The critical value determines how many standard errors we extend on either side of the sample mean.
Sample mean±t*×sn⏟Margin of error
\text{Sample mean} \ \pm \ \underbrace{t^* \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}}_{\text{Margin of error}}


s/ns/\sqrt{n} estimates the standard error, using the sample SD and sample size.
Because we estimate the population SD using the sample SD, we use a critical value, t*t^*, from the t distribution.
The critical value depends on the confidence level and sample size. For 12 students and 95% confidence, t*≈2.20t^* \approx 2.20.



Before walking through the formula: The general idea is the same whether we’re estimating a mean, a proportion, or a risk ratio: we use sample data to construct an interval that expresses uncertainty about a population parameter. The calculation depends on what we’re estimating, how the data were collected, and the assumptions we can make. Here, we’re estimating a population mean from a small sample with an unknown population standard deviation, so we’ll use a t-based confidence interval. For this example, we assume independent observations from an approximately normal population.
The t method also applies to larger samples when the population SD is unknown; it is not exclusively a small-sample method.
Build the formula from the sample mean and a margin of error. Both Excel workbooks use a two-sided t critical value with n−1 degrees of freedom. Here, n−1 = 11. Degrees of freedom account for estimating the mean from the same data and determine which t distribution we use.
A 95% interval uses a critical value that leaves 5% across the two tails of the t distribution, or 2.5% in each tail.
Using the displayed rounded values, the margin of error is approximately 2.20 × 1.05 = 2.31 points. Excel uses full precision to calculate the interval endpoints.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#excel-demo-repeated-confidence-intervals
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#excel-demo-repeated-confidence-intervals
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Excel Demo: Repeated Confidence Intervals
Open the prepared Excel sampling demonstration.

On Samples, trace one row from its 12 scores to its mean, SE, and interval.
Check whether its interval contains the population mean of 20.99.
On Coverage, compare the intervals from all 100 samples.

Will every interval capture the mean? Must exactly 95 of 100 capture it?


31–40 min across slides 14–15. Allow about four minutes to trace one row and five minutes to interpret the plot and coverage count.
Begin on Samples so students predict before seeing the Coverage summary. Row 8 is Sample 1. Its mean is 21.98, SD 5.39, SE 1.56, and 95% CI 18.55 to 25.40.
Columns O:Z hold the 12 linked scores. Columns B:J show n, mean, SD, SE, df, critical value, margin, and limits. Column K identifies capture or miss using the full-precision population mean.
The source population is approximately normal. Samples are independent draws; within each sample, selection is without replacement. With only 12 of 10,000 students, the finite-population correction is negligible. Coverage is approximate, not an exact guarantee for this finite population.
If Excel is unavailable, use the next slide’s plot and the example values in these notes.
Adapted from lab_warm_up_random_error.qmd, Confidence intervals section. Its original samples had 10 people; the approved adaptation uses 12.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#which-intervals-capture-the-population-mean
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#which-intervals-capture-the-population-mean
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: Which Intervals Capture the Population Mean?
text:
Which Intervals Capture the Population Mean?
Dots show sample means. Vertical lines show 95% confidence intervals.


98 of 100 capture the mean. Samples 13 and 63 miss it.



Ask students to find the two intervals that miss before revealing the count. The orange triangles and lines mark those samples; color is not the only cue.
The workbook compares full-precision endpoints with 20.987924. Labels are rounded for teaching.
Over many repetitions, the method captures the fixed mean about 95% of the time when its assumptions hold. This particular batch captures it 98% of the time. Another batch can have a different percentage.
Each completed interval either contains the population mean or does not. The 95% describes the method’s long-run coverage, not a probability assigned to this fixed parameter after observing one interval.
In a real study we do not know the population mean and cannot directly check capture. The simulation makes that otherwise hidden fact visible.
Adapted from random_error.pptx, slides 45 and 49–52, and lab_warm_up_random_error.qmd. This plot uses the approved workbook’s fixed samples.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-what-does-95-confidence-mean
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-what-does-95-confidence-mean
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Question: What Does 95% Confidence Mean?
A team reports a 95% confidence interval for mean StressScore. What does 95% describe?
A. The percentage of students whose scores fall inside the interval.
B. The long-run percentage of intervals from this method that capture the true mean.
C. The probability that the true mean is inside this particular interval.
D. The percentage of future sample means that fall inside this interval.


40–45 min across slides 16–17. Poll by show of fingers, one through four. Answer B, assuming the sampling and model conditions hold.
With repeated sampling, the interval changes while the population mean stays fixed. For any one computed interval, the true mean is either inside or outside.
Adapted from Random Error, slides 45 and 49–52.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-confidence-level-and-interval-width
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#question-confidence-level-and-interval-width
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: Question: Confidence Level and Interval Width
text:
Question: Confidence Level and Interval Width
The team uses the same 12 scores and the same method to calculate three confidence intervals. Which interval is widest?
A. The 90% confidence interval.
B. The 95% confidence interval.
C. The 99% confidence interval.
D. They all have the same width.


Answer C. On Samples, change M5 from 95% to 99%, then return to Coverage. The intervals widen and this batch captures the mean in 99 of 100 samples. Restore M5 to 95% afterward. Sample means, SDs, and SEs stay fixed.
Higher confidence requires a larger critical value and a wider interval when the data and method stay the same.
Ask students what they give up to obtain higher confidence: a narrower range of estimates. The SD and SE remain unchanged.
Adapted from Random Error quiz.docx, question 3. Corrected the source feedback, which reverses the relationship between confidence level and interval width. Higher alpha gives a narrower interval, all else equal.

objectID: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-makes-an-estimate-more-precise
href: Module 10 - Inferential Statistics—Estimation/Random Error and Confidence Intervals/Random Error and Confidence Intervals.html#what-makes-an-estimate-more-precise
title: Random Error and Confidence Intervals
section: What Makes an Estimate More Precise?
text:
What Makes an Estimate More Precise?
A smaller standard error means the sample estimate tends to vary less across repeated samples.

With the same sample SD and confidence level, a larger sample gives a narrower mean confidence interval.
With the same sample size and confidence level, a larger sample SD gives a wider interval.
For the same data, a higher confidence level gives a wider interval.


Instructions
- Open the Precision tab in the prepared Excel sampling demonstration. These are hypothetical comparisons using a mean of 21 and the rounded Prep 4 SD of 3.64, not newly drawn samples. Confidence is held at 95% across the three scenarios. - Compare Starting example with Larger sample: increasing n from 12 to 48 while holding SD fixed halves SE from about 1.05 to 0.53. The interval narrows from 18.69–23.31 to 19.94–22.06. Sample size also changes the t critical value through degrees of freedom, so the interval width is slightly less than half as large. - Compare Starting example with More variable scores: doubling SD from 3.64 to 7.28 while holding n fixed doubles SE and interval width. The interval becomes 16.37–25.63. - Ask students to predict each change before showing the results. The yellow starting inputs are editable; the other two scenarios update automatically. - Ask which condition is held fixed in each comparison. A narrow interval can still be centered on a biased estimate.

section: Prep 4 Worked Example: Comparing the Interval With the Population Norm
text:
Prep 4 Worked Example: Comparing the Interval With the Population Norm
Prep 4, Step 3 asks whether your population mean could equal a specified reference value. For practice, the assignment uses 20 for StressScore and 10 for AnxietyScore. These are hypothetical values.



Assigned Outcome
Hypothetical Population Norm




StressScore
20


AnxietyScore
10



The estimated mean is 21 points, with a 95% CI of 18.69 to 23.31. The interval includes the norm of 20, along with values below and above it.
The data are compatible with a population mean of 20 under the method’s assumptions. This does not establish that the true mean is 20.


55–60 min. The hypothetical comparison norm of 20 is separate from the sampling demonstration’s population mean of 20.99. Ask whether the result proves the mean is 20. The interval includes 20 along with other values compatible with the data and assumptions.
For Prep 4, students use the norm for their assigned outcome and explain their decision from the interval.
For the corresponding two-sided t test at the 0.05 level, we fail to reject a population mean of 20. Keep that decision distinct from proving the norm is correct or deciding whether a difference matters in practice.
Adapted from random_error.pptx, slides 31, 52–53, and Resources/Confidence Intervals.docx. Emphasize the estimate and full interval rather than only the test decision.

In a copy of the Prep 4 worked workbook, change the last score from 27 to 31.

Predict what will happen to the mean and to the interval width.
Record the new mean, sample SD, and 95% confidence interval.
Compare the new interval with the original. Is the estimate more or less precise? Does your decision about the norm of 20 change?



This is practice for outside of class.

60–72 min across slides 21–22. Allow about 8 minutes for group work and 4 minutes for comparison and discussion.
If Excel is unavailable, give groups the new mean (21.33), SE (1.26), and t critical value (2.20). Have them approximate the endpoints and explain the result.

Sleep = 5.0

Let’s start by orienting ourselves to the scatterplot.

X-axis: Sleep.

Y-axis: Stress score.


Questions - Ask a student to locate S01 and S02 and explain what each point represents.
- S01 = A
- S02 = C


What tends to happen to stress as we move left to right along the sleep axis?

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Four Things to Look For

Direction: upward, downward, or neither?
Strength: how closely do points follow a pattern?
Form: approximately straight or curved?
Unusual observations: does a point stand apart?



Now that we are oriented to scatterplots, there are at least four characteristics of scatterplots that deserve our attention. Let’s talk about each of them in turn.

We’ll start with direction.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#direction-of-the-relationship
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#direction-of-the-relationship
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Direction of the Relationship



Positive: higher X tends to accompany higher Y.

Negative: higher X tends to accompany lower Y.



Review: positive and negative describe direction, not whether a relationship is good or bad.
No clear linear pattern does not rule out other kinds of relationships.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-1
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-1
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Four Things to Look For

Direction: upward, downward, or neither?
Strength: how closely do points follow a pattern?



The second is strength: how closely do the points follow a pattern?

More specifically, for a linear relationship, how closely do the points follow a straight-line pattern?

Imagine drawing a straight line through each cloud of points. Strength concerns how closely the points follow that line. The line’s slope describes its direction and steepness.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#strength-of-the-relationship
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#strength-of-the-relationship
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Strength of the Relationship

All three have the same underlying slope. They differ in how tightly the points cluster around it.


A steep slope is not the same as a strong relationship. Strength concerns how tightly points follow the pattern, not the axis units or steepness.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#question-which-relationship-is-stronger
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#question-which-relationship-is-stronger
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Question: Which Relationship Is Stronger?












Which shows a stronger linear relationship?
A. Plot A
B. Plot B
C. Both are equally strong
D. Cannot tell from the plots
Choose one and explain why.



Answer: A. All of its points lie on a straight line, even though the line rises gently.
Plot B has a steeper upward pattern, but its points scatter around that pattern.
Both plots use the same X values and identical axis scales. Steepness describes the slope; strength describes how closely the points follow a straight-line pattern.
Ask students who choose B to explain what they noticed, then distinguish steepness from strength. No calculation is needed to identify the perfect linear relationship in Plot A.

title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Four Things to Look For

Direction: upward, downward, or neither?
Strength: how closely do points follow a pattern?
Form: approximately straight or curved?



The third is form. Is the cloud of points approximately straight or curved?

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#a-relationship-can-be-nonlinear
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#a-relationship-can-be-nonlinear
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
A Relationship Can Be Nonlinear












This U-shaped pattern is one example of a nonlinear relationship. Other patterns may rise and then fall, or level off.



The pattern is clear, but it does not follow a straight line.

As X increases, Y first decreases and then increases. Look at the whole pattern: a relationship can be clear without following a straight line.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-3
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-3
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Four Things to Look For

Direction: upward, downward, or neither?
Strength: how closely do points follow a pattern?
Form: approximately straight or curved?
Unusual observations: does a point stand apart?



The fourth is unusual observations. Do any values stand out as unusual or possible errors?

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#unusual-observations
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#unusual-observations
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Unusual Observations













Which observation stands apart from the overall pattern?
What would you want to check?




Check whether the values were recorded correctly, how sleep and stress were measured, and whether the student’s circumstances could plausibly explain the observation. We cannot identify an error from the plot alone.

An unusual observation is worth investigating. It is not automatically an error.

Do not automatically remove a legitimate observation because it stands apart. We will return to this example when discussing how an observation can affect a correlation.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-4
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#four-things-to-look-for-4
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Four Things to Look For

Direction: upward, downward, or neither?
Strength: how closely do points follow a pattern?
Form: approximately straight or curved?
Unusual observations: does a point stand apart?



Prep 3 asks for direction, apparent strength, and possible influential outliers. Checking form makes those descriptions more defensible.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#pearsons-correlation-coefficient
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#pearsons-correlation-coefficient
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient
r ranges from −1 to +1.



Feature
Interpretation




Sign
Direction of the linear relationship


Absolute value
Strength of the linear relationship


Near −1 or +1
Points lie close to a straight line


Near 0
Little linear relationship





Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient is one statistic we can use to do so.

Minutes 16-19: r is unitless. It is not a change in stress points per hour of sleep.
An r of -0.8 is stronger in absolute magnitude than an r of +0.3.
Avoid universal weak/moderate/strong cutoffs. The context and scatterplot matter.
Pearson’s r requires variation in both variables. A constant variable has no defined Pearson correlation.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#question-which-relationship-is-strongest
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#question-which-relationship-is-strongest
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Question: Which Relationship Is Strongest?
Consider these correlation coefficients:
A. r = +0.35
B. r = −0.80
C. r = +0.60
D. r = −0.10


Answer: B. Its absolute value, 0.80, is closest to 1.
The negative sign describes direction. It does not make the relationship weaker.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#similar-r-different-patterns
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#similar-r-different-patterns
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Similar r, Different Patterns

Both have r ≈ 0.816. A single coefficient does not show the shape.


Which has a stronger relationship?

Both values round to 0.816.

Why do they have the same r value? Pearson’s correlation coefficient only measures the strength of linear relationships.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#one-observation-can-change-r
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#one-observation-can-change-r
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
One Observation Can Change r

Original r = -0.834. With the added observation, r = -0.077.


Unusual observations can strengthen, weaken, or reverse a correlation depending on their location.
Check recording, measurement, and context. Do not delete a legitimate observation merely to improve r.
A point is influential when it materially affects the result; being unusual and being influential are related but distinct ideas.

When we view many pairwise correlations, they will sometimes be presented as a matrix like this one.

Read the sleep-stress cell first, then the stress-screen-time cell.
The diagonal is 1 because each nonconstant variable correlates perfectly with itself.
The matrix is symmetric because swapping X and Y does not change r.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#correlation-and-causation
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#correlation-and-causation
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Correlation and Causation












Students who sleep more might report less stress because:

Sleep affects stress.
Stress affects sleep.
Workload or another factor affects both.




We might be tempted to conclude that there is a causal relationship between stress and sleep. And there may be.

However, this scatterplot alone cannot distinguish these explanations.
Measuring sleep and stress during the same week does not establish their temporal ordering.
A large correlation does not remove confounding, selection concerns, or measurement error.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Predicting Stress












Now, suppose we want to predict a student’s stress score.
Without knowledge of their sleep duration, what is our best prediction?

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress-with-the-mean
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress-with-the-mean
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Predicting Stress With the Mean













Without using sleep, our best prediction is the mean stress score for everyone:


21.65 points.


Each vertical segment shows an observed score’s distance from that prediction.




Now, suppose we want to predict a student’s stress score, but we do not use their sleep duration. We could use the average stress score for all 20 students. Everyone would get the same prediction.
The horizontal dashed line is that mean. Point to S01 at 5 hours and 28 points. Its observed score is above the prediction, so its prediction error is positive. Scores below the line have negative errors.
Ask: Would knowing how much each student sleeps help us make better predictions for these students?
To summarize the errors, square each vertical distance and add them. Squaring prevents positive and negative errors from canceling. Their sum is the total variation in stress around the mean.
Reference: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat501/Lesson01

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress-with-sleep
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#predicting-stress-with-sleep
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Predicting Stress With Sleep












The regression line predicts stress using sleep duration.
The vertical segments now show errors relative to the line.



But we already know that sleep and stress are associated. And what does it mean when two variables are associated?

A simple linear regression uses a straight line to describe the predicted mean outcome at each value of one predictor. Here stress is the outcome and sleep is the predictor.

The least-squares line is chosen to minimize the sum of squared vertical errors. Students do not need to fit the line or calculate its slope in this lesson.

The dashed horizontal line is the previous mean-only prediction. The solid purple line uses sleep. The sum of squared errors gets smaller, although an individual student’s error can get larger.
Reference: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat501/Lesson01

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#from-r-to-r²
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#from-r-to-r²
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
From r to r²
r², the coefficient of determination, measures the proportion of variation accounted for by the regression line.



Prediction
Sum of Squared Errors




Mean only
404.55


Regression line
122.99



r2=1−122.99404.55≈0.696r^2 = 1 - \frac{122.99}{404.55} \approx 0.696
Using sleep reduces the sum of squared errors by 69.6% compared with using the mean alone.
For simple linear regression with an intercept, this also equals Pearson’s r squared.


The mean-only prediction gives us about 404.55 squared points of error. Using sleep lowers that to about 122.99. The fraction left is about 30.4%. Subtract that from 100%, and we find that the line accounts for about 69.6% of the original variation.
The sums use squared stress-score points. Their ratio is unitless. Values displayed here are rounded, but all calculations use full precision.
Squaring the full-precision Pearson correlation gives the same result: r ≈ -0.834, and r² ≈ 0.696. This equality applies to simple least-squares regression with an intercept.
r² has no sign. Keep r to describe direction.
Explained variation is statistical, not proof of causation. It is not a percentage of people, prediction accuracy, or a reduction in stress scores.
The remainder is variation not accounted for by this linear relationship; it is not proof that specific other causes have been identified.
Reference: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat501/Lesson01

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#why-we-can-square-r
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Scatterplots and Correlation/Scatterplots and Correlation.html#why-we-can-square-r
title: Scatterplots and Correlation
text:
Why We Can Square r
For ordinary least-squares regression:

Simple means one predictor: sleep duration.
With an intercept means the line can shift up or down instead of being forced through (0, 0).

Under these conditions, both calculations give the same r²:


Square the correlation
(−0.834253)2≈0.696(-0.834253)^2 \approx 0.696

Compare squared errors
1−122.99404.55≈0.6961 - \frac{122.99}{404.55} \approx 0.696

r retains direction. r² describes the proportion of variation accounted for by the line.


For the straight-line model we’re using here, squaring the correlation gives us exactly the same proportion we calculated by comparing prediction errors. That’s why we can calculate r² in Excel simply by squaring r.
This agreement is a mathematical property of ordinary least-squares regression with one predictor and an intercept, not a coincidence in these data. Both calculations use the same paired observations and full-precision values. The displayed numbers are rounded.
Write the model if useful: Stresŝ=b0+b1(Sleep)\widehat{\text{Stress}} = b_0 + b_1(\text{Sleep}). The hat means predicted stress. The slope, b1b_1, describes how predicted stress changes with sleep duration.
The intercept, b0b_0, lets the line move up or down. It is the predicted stress at zero hours of sleep, but zero is outside our observed range, so we should not give that prediction a substantive interpretation here.
With an intercept, the least-squares line passes through the point defined by the sample mean of sleep and the sample mean of stress. This property supports the connection between correlation and the reduction in squared errors.
r describes the direction and strength of the linear relationship. Squaring removes its sign: r = −0.80 and r = +0.80 both give r² = 0.64. Their directions differ, but the proportion of variation accounted for is the same.
If we force the line through the origin by removing the intercept, this equality generally does not hold. With multiple predictors, the model’s R² generally differs from the squared correlation between the outcome and any single predictor.
The proportion describes variation accounted for in the data used to fit the line. It does not establish causation or guarantee prediction accuracy for new students.
Reference: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat501/Lesson01

Calculate r in Excel
In G3 on Practice, enter:
=CORREL(B2:B21,C2:C21)
Result: r = -0.834.
More sleep accompanies lower stress in this sample, with a fairly strong negative linear relationship.


Minutes 65-68: demonstrate after the visual interpretation exercise.
Both ranges refer to the same students in the same order. Do not include headers or the summary cells.
CORREL returns r, not a p-value. We will address inference later.

About 69.6% of the variation in stress scores is accounted for by the linear relationship with sleep.


Minutes 68-70: calculate r² from the full-precision cell rather than squaring a rounded display value.
Connect this result to the mean-versus-line comparison: the fitted line reduced the sum of squared errors from 404.55 to 122.99, a reduction of about 69.6%. Squaring r in Excel gives that same proportion.
COUNT(B2:B21) gives the pair count here because both columns are complete and numeric. It is not a general check for paired missingness.
The percentage describes variation in this sample. It does not say sleep caused that percentage of stress or explain that percentage of individual students.

title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Average Sleep Duration
Across all 150 respondents in the fictional TCU survey, the average is 6.2 hours per night.

What conclusions can the group draw from these data?



Statistics help us to summarize and make sense of raw data.

The stated 6.2-hour mean describes all 150 fictional respondents, not just the 12 shown on the previous slide.
Invite students to suggest a defensible sentence and a sentence that goes too far.
Ask how the respondents were recruited and what “per night” means.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#what-statistics-adds
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#what-statistics-adds
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
What Statistics Adds







Question
What we need




What did we observe?
Counts, percentages, summaries, and graphs


How much do observations differ?
Measures of spread


What might this tell us about a population?
Sampling information and statistical inference





Connect the individual sleep responses and their mean to the first row: statistics help us summarize raw data.
Connect to the familiar epidemiologic questions of occurrence, distribution, and association.
Statistical methods organize and evaluate evidence; they do not guarantee accurate measurements or remove selection bias.
Precision and hypothesis testing will receive dedicated lessons later.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#target-population-source-population-and-sample
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#target-population-source-population-and-sample
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
section: Target Population, Source Population, and Sample
text:
Target Population, Source Population, and Sample
Suppose the survey recruits students leaving the library one evening.








Group
Who belongs to it?
In our example




Target population
People we want findings to apply to
All students enrolled at TCU in Fall 2026


Source population
People from whom we select participants
TCU students leaving that library that evening


Study sample
People whose data we analyze
The 150 students who respond to the survey



How well might these respondents represent all TCU students?


The library recruitment setting is a hypothetical addition to the fictional survey scenario.
Define the population by membership and time.
Ask which students this recruitment setting might miss and whether respondents could differ from students who decline to participate.
Distinguish the source population from the sample: not everyone leaving the library necessarily responds.
A larger sample from this source would not automatically make it representative of all TCU students.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#descriptive-and-inferential-statistics
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#descriptive-and-inferential-statistics
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Descriptive and Inferential Statistics
Descriptive Statistics
Describe the sample we observed.
Inferential Statistics
Use sample data to make inferences about the target population.


Connect to the preceding slide: we describe the 150 respondents, then ask what their data can tell us about all TCU students enrolled in Fall 2026.
Sampling error is chance variation: another random sample could have a different mean sleep duration even with sound sampling. It does not mean someone made a mistake.
Bias is systematic error. Recruiting only at one library, differences between respondents and nonrespondents, or inaccurate sleep reports could distort the estimate. A larger sample does not automatically remove these problems.
Confounding becomes relevant when we interpret the sleep–stress association, especially as a possible causal effect. For example, workload could influence both sleep and stress and help explain their association. Confounding is not the central concern when estimating mean sleep duration alone.
Inferential methods quantify uncertainty under assumptions about how the data were collected and analyzed. They do not automatically correct bias or confounding.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#question-describing-or-inferring
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#question-describing-or-inferring
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Question: Describing or Inferring?
Statement A
“The 150 respondents reported an average of 6.2 hours of sleep.”
Statement B
“We estimate the average sleep duration of all TCU students from the sample.”

Which statement describes observed data? Which makes an inference?
What would you need to know before trusting Statement B?



Give pairs 2 minutes, then collect two responses.
Statement A is descriptive: it summarizes the respondents. Statement B is inferential: it uses their data to estimate a characteristic of all TCU students.
Expected issues: recruitment, nonresponse, whether different student groups were represented, the measurement question, and the period measured.
Connect to the library example: students leaving one library on one evening may differ from the target population, and respondents may differ from nonrespondents.
Samples can vary even with a sound sampling process; a biased recruitment process is a separate concern.
Adapted from the think–pair–share activity on slide 9 of Yan Zhang’s Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics PowerPoint. The TCU setting and 6.2-hour mean are fictional adaptations; the source uses percentages of students reporting poor sleep.
Low-tech fallback: pair discussion and verbal responses.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#population-and-sample-summaries
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#population-and-sample-summaries
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Population and Sample Summaries
We use the mean sleep duration in our sample to estimate the mean in our target population.
What do we call a numerical summary of a population? Of a sample?










Target population
Sample




Numerical summary
Parameter
Statistic


Example
Mean sleep for all TCU students
Mean sleep for 150 respondents


Mean symbol
μ\mu
x‾\bar{x}



A sample statistic can estimate a population parameter.



Connect to Statement B on the previous slide: the sample mean is known, and we use it to estimate the unknown mean for the target population.
Ask the class to recall both terms before revealing the table. Expected answers: population parameter and sample statistic.
After revealing the table, connect the terms to the mean symbols: mu for the population mean and x-bar for the sample mean.
Adapted from Yan slides 15-16.
Emphasize what group is summarized, rather than memorizing a Greek-versus-Roman rule.
Not all parameter symbols are Greek.
The population parameter is fixed for the defined population and measurement period; a statistic can vary from sample to sample.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#question-statistic-or-parameter
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#question-statistic-or-parameter
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Question: Statistic or Parameter?

The mean sleep duration among 150 surveyed TCU students is 6.2 hours. What is 6.2 hours?


A. A population parameter
B. A sample statistic
C. Both
D. Neither



Answer: B. The mean summarizes the 150 respondents.
The mean for all enrolled TCU students would be a population parameter.
A statistic may estimate a parameter, but the two need not be equal.
Allow 3 minutes, including discussion.
Have students write A, B, C, or D on paper, compare with a partner, then vote by raising fingers.
Discuss the reason before revealing the answer.

What Is a Variable?
How would you define a variable? Give one example from a student health survey.

A variable is a characteristic that can take different values across observations.



One student
Values recorded




Sleep duration
6.5 hours per night


High stress reported
Yes


Stress rating
High


Number of caffeinated drinks yesterday
2






Variable block: 12 minutes through “Choose a Summary.”
Ask the class for a definition and one or two examples before revealing the definition and table.
Listen for the distinction between a variable and its value: sleep duration is a variable; 6.5 hours is one recorded value.
Each row here describes a different variable measured on the same fictional person, rather than four people.
In a usual dataset, one student occupies one row and each variable has a column.
The high-stress response is a binary self-report, not a diagnosis.
Adapted from Yan slides 17-19 and Friis Chapter 2, Variables, Data, and Measurement Scales.

Review: Categorical Variables
What are the two types of categorical variables? How do they differ?









Kind
Distinction
Example




Nominal
Categories without a natural order
Major; yes/no response


Ordinal
Categories with an order
Low/moderate/high stress



A numerical code does not automatically make a category quantitative.



Ask students to call out the two types, explain the difference, and offer an example before revealing the table.
A binary variable has two categories.
For example, 0 = no and 1 = yes remains a categorical response.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#review-quantitative-variables
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#review-quantitative-variables
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Review: Quantitative Variables
What are the two types of quantitative variables? How do they differ?









Kind
Distinction
Example




Discrete quantitative
Countable numerical values
Number of drinks


Continuous quantitative
Measurements along a continuum
Sleep duration






Ask students to call out the two types, explain the difference, and offer an example before revealing the table.
Recorded sleep may be rounded to half-hours, but duration is the underlying continuous quantity.
Do not classify counts as continuous.
Interval and ratio describe another aspect of measurement: equal intervals and whether zero has a meaningful interpretation.
If asked, temperature in Celsius is interval, while elapsed duration has a meaningful zero.
Keep this distinction brief rather than adding another taxonomy lesson.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#classify-the-recorded-values
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data/Statistical Thinking and Describing Data.html#classify-the-recorded-values
title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Classify the Recorded Values
Classify each variable.

Caffeine use: yes / no
Sleep duration: 5.5 / 6.0 / 7.5 hours
Stress rating: low / moderate / high
Number of nights studied past midnight: 0 / 1 / 2 / … / 7



Allow about 3 minutes for whole-class discussion. Ask for a classification and a brief explanation for each variable.
Answers: nominal binary, continuous quantitative, ordinal, discrete quantitative.
The wording and recorded values determine the classification.
A numeric stress score is not the same variable as a low/moderate/high stress category; use the project’s codebook when interpreting the actual score.
If responses differ, ask students to explain which recorded values support their classification before confirming the answer.

text:
Question: Which Denominator?

Of 12 fictional students, 6 report less than 7 hours of sleep. Of those 6, 4 report high stress. What percentage of the shorter-sleep group reports high stress?


A. 4 / 12 = 33.3%
B. 6 / 12 = 50.0%
C. 4 / 6 = 66.7%
D. 6 / 4 = 150.0%



Answer: C. The question restricts the denominator to the 6 students in the shorter-sleep group.
Four of those 6 report high stress.
The fraction 4/12 answers a different question: what proportion of the whole sample is in both categories?
Allow 4 minutes, including discussion.
Have students write A, B, C, or D on paper, compare with a partner, then vote by raising fingers.
Discuss the reason before revealing the answer.

text:
How Would We Summarize Sleep Hours?
We have described categories using counts and percentages.
What should we ask about the continuous sleep measurements to summarize them?


What is a typical value? Center
How different are the values? Spread
What does the distribution look like? Shape




Ask the class for the questions we should ask about continuous data before revealing the bullets. Accept everyday language, then connect their responses to center, spread, and shape.
Use the final 2 minutes of the group block to connect its categorical summaries to continuous summaries.
This is only an introduction to center and spread; the next meeting develops these concepts and their spreadsheet procedures.

title: Statistical Thinking and Describing Data
text:
Review: Mean, Median, and Mode
Sorted sleep hours:
5, 5.5, 6, 6, 6.5, 6.5, 7, 7, 7.5, 8, 8, 9
Calculate the mean, median, and mode.

Mean: total hours ÷ number of students = 6.83 hours
Median: average of the two middle values = 6.75 hours
Modes: 6, 6.5, 7, and 8 hours — each appears twice.



Center/spread block: 8 minutes through “The Same Mean Can Hide Different Spread.”
Give students about 2 minutes to calculate all three summaries; calculators are welcome. Ask for their answers and reasoning before revealing the solutions.
Have students locate the middle positions before discussing the answer: the 6th and 7th values are 6.5 and 7, giving 6.75.
The total is 82 hours, so 82/12 = 6.8333.
Do not require a long hand-calculation exercise.
The mode is the most frequent value or category; this dataset has several tied modal values (6, 6.5, 7, and 8).
Its tied modes are a useful reason not to force a single mode or infer skew from a mean/median/mode ordering.

Calculate the range for each group. Which group has more spread?


Ask students to calculate both ranges and explain which group varies more before revealing the table.
Group A: 8 − 6 = 2 hours. Group B: 10 − 4 = 6 hours.
Both means are 7, but group B varies more.
Range is maximum minus minimum.
Introduce SD as a measure of spread around the mean and IQR as the spread of the middle half of values; defer calculation and detailed interpretation to Wednesday.

This is a small conceptual check with a verbal-response fallback.
Do not infer distribution shape from only three observations.
