title: Case-Control Studies
text:
When Cohort Is Not Ideal
Cohort studies are powerful — but not always practical.

What if:

The disease is rare?
The outcome has a long latency period?
Long-term follow-up is too costly or infeasible?
You need results quickly?
In these situations, a different design may be more efficient.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#induction-and-latent-periods
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#induction-and-latent-periods
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Induction and Latent Periods



The induction period is the time from exposure to disease initiation. In this diagram, disease begins when the sufficient cause is complete.
The latent period is the time from disease initiation to detection, shown here as diagnosis. Disease can be present before we detect it.
The key idea is that exposure, disease initiation, symptoms, and diagnosis can occur at different times. A cohort study may need a long follow-up period to observe the outcome.
Source: cohort_studies.pptx, slide 23. The original slide notes cite Kenneth J. Rothman, Epidemiology: An Introduction, p. 81.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#basic-case-control-study-design
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#basic-case-control-study-design
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Basic Case-Control Study Design



Here’s my graphical representation of the basic case-control study design. There are other case-control designs, but this gives us an intuitive starting point.
Exposures and outcomes occur out in the world. We then identify a group of people who have experienced the outcome of interest, called cases, and measure their history of exposure.
We also identify a comparison group without the outcome, called controls, from the population that gave rise to the cases. We measure their history of exposure in the same way.
Finally, we calculate the odds of prior exposure in each group and compare those odds.
In this example, orange represents exposure to smoking and blue represents no exposure to smoking. Triangles represent people with lung cancer, and circles represent people without lung cancer.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#retrospective-cohort-vs.-case-control
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#retrospective-cohort-vs.-case-control
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Retrospective Cohort vs. Case-Control

Case-control

Sample based on outcome and look backward for exposure.

Retrospective Cohort

Sample based on exposure and look “forward” towards the outcome
A cohort study was done. You just weren’t there to initially observe it



Don’t confuse retrospective cohort and case-control.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#study-base-principle
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#study-base-principle
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Study Base Principle

Cases and controls should be “representative of the same base experience.”
If a potential control had gotten the disease, they would have been selected with the same probability as any other case.




Selecting controls can be one of the trickiest parts of using case-control studies. It starts with the study base principle.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#recall-bias
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#recall-bias
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Recall Bias




Definition: A type of information bias in which participants remember past exposures differently.
When it occurs

Often in case-control studies
Cases may recall exposures more carefully than controls

Key idea: Differences in memory between groups can distort the exposure–outcome association.





Recall bias is another important threat to validity when conducting case-control studies.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#interviewer-and-observer-bias
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#interviewer-and-observer-bias
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Interviewer and Observer Bias


Interviewer Bias

Occurs during data collection
Interviewer knowledge influences how questions are asked
Can lead to different responses between groups

Observer Bias

Occurs during outcome assessment
Observer expectations influence how outcomes are recorded
More likely when blinding is absent

Key idea: When researchers influence data collection or measurement, results may be systematically distorted.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#why-use-an-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#why-use-an-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Why Use an Odds Ratio?


In case-control studies, we cannot calculate risk directly. Why?

We start with a fixed number of cases and controls
The total population at risk is unknown
Incidence cannot be measured
Instead, we quantify association using the Odds Ratio (OR)

What Does OR Measure?

The odds of prior exposure among cases compared to the odds of exposure among controls

Key Contrast:

Cohort → Uses Relative Risk (RR)
Case-Control → Uses Odds Ratio (OR)

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#odds-of-exposure-among-cases
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#odds-of-exposure-among-cases
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Odds of Exposure Among Cases
Given the prototypical 2x2 table for case-control data, which of the formulas below will calculate the odds of exposure among cases?





Cases
Controls




Exposed
A
B


Not exposed
C
D









A. \(\frac{a}{c}\)

B. \(\frac{a}{b}\)

C. \(\frac{a}{a+b}\)

D. \(\frac{a}{a+c}\)


Do you remember how to calculate and interpret odds?

Do you remember how to calculate and interpret an odds ratio?

Let’s have a little refresher.
The odds of exposure among cases can be calculated as a / c.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#odds-of-exposure-among-cases-1
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#odds-of-exposure-among-cases-1
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Odds of Exposure Among Cases
Given the prototypical 2x2 table for case-control data, which of the following is an accurate expression of the odds of exposure among cases?





Cases
Controls




Exposed
50
25


Not exposed
100
100


Odds of exposure
???






The odds of exposure among cases = \(a/c = 50/100 = 0.5\).
Equivalent ways to express these odds: 50:100 = 0.5:1 = 5:10 = 1:2.
For every 1 exposed case, there are 2 unexposed cases.



And we can express the odds in many different ways.
For example, as a over c or as a to c. In this particular case, that translates to 50 over 100 or 50 to 100. Or, if we divide 50 by 100, we get 0.5, which we can also express as 0.5 to 1. In other words, for every 0.5 cases who were exposed, there was one who wasn’t exposed.
If we move the decimal one place to the right on both sides of our ratio (multiply by 10), we get 5 to 10, and we can say for every 5 cases who were exposed, there were 10 cases who were not exposed.
We could also divide one by the odds (0.5) and add the result to the right-hand side of the ratio. We could then say for every case who was exposed, there were 2 cases who were not exposed. As you can see, we can get the same answer by dividing 100 by 50 and putting the answer on the right-hand side of the ratio.
All of these are equivalent ways of expressing the odds of exposure among cases.

The only correct expression of the odds among the choices above is 0.25. You can derive this answer by dividing 25 by 100.

Controls

50 / 100
25 / 100





Odds of exposure among cases = 50 / 100 = 0.5
Odds of exposure among controls = 25 / 100 = 0.25



Now that we’ve calculated the odds of exposure among cases and controls, we may want to compare them in order to say something about the association (or lack thereof) between exposure and outcome – or being a case.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#association
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#association
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Association


The distribution of the thing we are measuring differs, on average, between two groups. This could be its center, spread, shape, or the proportion of people in each category.
Knowing something about X tells us something about Y.




And remember that an association exists when the distribution of the thing we are measuring is different, on average, in two groups. Alternatively, we can say that knowing something about x tells us something about y or helps us predict y.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#comparing-exposure-odds
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#comparing-exposure-odds
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Comparing Exposure Odds





Cases
Controls

50

100
100

50 / 100
25 / 100





Odds of exposure among cases = 0.5
Odds of exposure among controls = 0.25

The odds are higher among cases. How much higher?


We can tell just by looking at the odds, which are 0.5 and 0.25, that they aren’t the same. That is, the odds of being exposed if you are a case are greater than the odds of being exposed if you are a control. But, how much greater?

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#calculating-the-exposure-odds-ratio

\[
\text{Exposure OR} = \frac{\text{Odds of exposure among cases}}{\text{Odds of exposure among controls}} = \frac{a/c}{b/d}
\]


Well, we can answer that question by calculating the ratio of the odds among cases to the odds among controls.

How would you interpret this odds ratio?


So, our exposure OR is 2. And how do we interpret that?

25 / 100




\[
\text{Exposure OR} = \frac{50/100}{25/100} = \frac{0.5}{0.25} = 2
\]
The odds of exposure among cases are 2 times the odds of exposure among controls.


The odds of exposure among cases are 2 times the odds of exposure among controls.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#why-use-the-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#why-use-the-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Why Use the Odds Ratio?






Cases
Controls




Exposed
50
25


Not exposed
100
100


Odds of exposure
50 / 100
25 / 100





We can calculate it directly from a case-control study.
We can also estimate it using logistic regression.
Under certain conditions, it approximates the risk ratio.



And the odds ratio has some really convenient traits that make it an attractive measure of association when we have data from a case-control study.
Unlike the incidence proportion ratio, the odds ratio can be directly calculated from a case-based case-control study.
It can be derived from logistic regression models.
It can be used to approximate the incidence proportion ratio under certain conditions. And as we’ve said before, the incidence proportion ratio is generally considered to be a more intuitive measure of association.
Therefore, we will briefly compare the odds ratio and the incidence proportion ratio.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#hypothetical-cohort-hypertension-and-mi
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#hypothetical-cohort-hypertension-and-mi
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Hypothetical Cohort: Hypertension and MI


One-year incidence of acute myocardial infarction (MI, or heart attack). Severe systolic hypertension: ≥180 mm Hg. Normal systolic blood pressure: <120 mm Hg.





MI (+)
MI (–)
Total




Severe hypertension
180
9,820
10,000


Normotensive
30
9,970
10,000





Risk of MI among people with severe hypertension = 180 / 10,000 = 0.018
Risk of MI among normotensive people = 30 / 10,000 = 0.003
Risk ratio (incidence proportion ratio) = 0.018 / 0.003 = 6
Participants with severe hypertension had 6 times the risk of MI over one year compared with normotensive participants.




mmHg is said as “millimeters of mercury.”
Sometimes, it’s helpful to start by discussing a cohort study. In the example shown here, severe hypertension and acute myocardial infarction are the exposure and the outcome of interest, respectively.
Because this is a cohort study and we know the row totals, we can calculate the incidence proportion ratio as we’ve done all semester. In this case, participants with severe hypertension had 6 times the risk of MI over the 1-year study period compared to participants with normotensive blood pressure.
For these data, the risk of myocardial infarction is relatively low for both the exposed and unexposed groups. Specifically, the risk of MI is 0.018 among those with severe hypertension and 0.003 among people with normotensive blood pressure.
Therefore, the odds of developing MI will approximate the probabilities; as a result, the odds ratio of disease approximates the incidence proportion ratio.
Why?



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#risk-and-odds
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#risk-and-odds
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Risk and Odds





Outcome
No outcome
Total




Exposed
a
b
a + b


Unexposed
c
d
c + d














Measure
Formula
a = 0
Incidence = 0.001




Incidence
\(\frac{a}{a+b}\)
\(\frac{0}{0+b}=0\)
\(0.001\)


Odds
\(\frac{\frac{a}{a+b}}{1-\frac{a}{a+b}}\)
\(\frac{\frac{0}{0+b}}{1-\frac{0}{0+b}} = \frac{0}{1-0} = \frac{0}{1} = 0\)
\(\frac{0.001}{1-0.001} \approx \frac{0.001}{1}\)




Risk in the exposed: \(p = a/(a+b)\). Odds in the exposed: \(p/(1-p) = a/b\).
When risk is small, 1 − risk is close to 1, so odds and risk are similar.


Because the odds are calculated as the incidence over 1 minus the incidence. When the risk is really low, 1 minus the incidence is very close to 1-0, or 1, and any number divided by 1 is that number. So, you basically end up with the incidence divided by 1, which is just the incidence.
As an extreme example, if a is 0, then the incidence in the exposed is 0. Likewise, the odds in the exposed are 0 divided by 1 minus zero, which is 0 divided by 1, which is also zero. In this case, the odds equal the incidence.
Now, as a slightly less extreme example, let’s imagine the incidence is 0.001 or 1 in 1,000. In this case, the denominator is almost 1 (0.999 to be exact), and therefore, the odds are almost identical to the incidence.
So, the lower the incidence, the closer 1 minus the incidence is to one, and therefore, the better the incidence and the odds approximate each other. As the outcome becomes less rare, the OR will generally become increasingly more extreme than the IPR.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#comparing-the-risk-ratio-and-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#comparing-the-risk-ratio-and-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
section: Comparing the Risk Ratio and Odds Ratio
text:
Comparing the Risk Ratio and Odds Ratio





MI (+)
MI (–)
Total




Severe hypertension
180
9,820
10,000


Normotensive
30
9,970
10,000





The incidence of MI among people with severe hypertension = 180 / 10,000 = 0.018
The incidence of MI among people who are normotensive = 30 / 10,000 = 0.003
Risk ratio = 0.018 / 0.003 = 6 
The odds of severe hypertension among cases = 180 / 30 = 6
The odds of severe hypertension among controls = 9,820 / 9,970 ≈ 0.985
Exposure OR = (180 / 30) / (9,820 / 9,970) ≈ 6.09




And although we would typically calculate the incidence proportion ratio as our measure of association from cohort data like this, we can also calculate the odds ratio. In this case, the exposure odds ratio is 6.09 – similar to the incidence proportion ratio.
And how would we interpret that odds ratio?



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#hypertension-and-mi-interpreting-the-or
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#hypertension-and-mi-interpreting-the-or
title: Case-Control Studies
section: Hypertension and MI: Interpreting the OR
text:
Hypertension and MI: Interpreting the OR





MI (+)
MI (–)
Total




Severe hypertension
180
9,820
10,000


Normotensive
30
9,970
10,000





Exposure odds among cases = 180 / 30 = 6
Exposure odds among non-cases = 9,820 / 9,970 ≈ 0.985
Exposure OR = (180 / 30) / (9,820 / 9,970) ≈ 6.09

Participants with MI had 6.09 times the odds of severe hypertension compared with participants who did not have an MI during the one-year study period.



We could say participants with MI had 6.09 times the odds of severe hypertension compared to participants who did not have an MI over the 1-year study period.
Okay, great. The odds ratio approximates the incidence proportion ratio. But, why not just always calculate the incidence proportion ratio to begin with?
Again, here we know the total number of participants who were exposed and who were unexposed in these cohort study data – 10,000 each – but in a typical case-based case-control study we don’t have that information. That’s the basic reason we can’t just keep calculating the more intuitive incidence proportion ratio.



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#sampling-10-of-controls

title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Sampling 10% of Controls





MI (+)
MI (–)
Cohort total




Severe hypertension
180
982
??


Normotensive
30
997
??





Population risks require the original cohort denominators: 180 / ?? and 30 / ??.
Exposure odds among cases = 180 / 30 = 6
Exposure odds among sampled controls = 982 / 997 ≈ 0.985
Exposure OR = (180 / 30) / (982 / 997) ≈ 6.09

The OR is unchanged when we sample the same fraction of exposed and unexposed non-cases.



For this illustration, keep all cases and take exactly 10% of the exposed non-cases and 10% of the unexposed non-cases. The control counts become 982 and 997.
The row sums in the case-control sample are not the original cohort denominators. Without those denominators or sampling information that lets us reconstruct them, we cannot calculate the population risks directly.
Here we know the sampling fraction because we created this example from a complete cohort. In a typical case-control study, we do not have that complete cohort information.
The odds of exposure among controls remain 982 / 997 = 9,820 / 9,970. Therefore, the exposure odds ratio is unchanged at approximately 6.09. Random sampling may introduce sampling error.



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#disease-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#disease-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Disease Odds Ratio





MI (+)
MI (–)
Cohort total




Severe hypertension
180
9,820
??


Normotensive
30
9,970
??





Disease odds with severe hypertension = 180 / 9,820 ≈ 0.01833
Disease odds with normal blood pressure = 30 / 9,970 ≈ 0.003009
Disease OR = (180 / 9,820) / (30 / 9,970) ≈ 6.09

Participants with severe hypertension had 6.09 times the odds of MI over one year compared with normotensive participants.



The exposure odds ratio and disease odds ratio are algebraically identical: (a/c) / (b/d) = (a/b) / (c/d) = ad/bc.
Here we use the full counts from the hypothetical cohort. We retain the unknown cohort totals to show that calculating the odds ratio does not require those denominators.
Participants with severe hypertension had 6.09 times the odds of MI compared with normotensive participants over the one-year study period. This disease-focused interpretation is generally the one of greater interest.
Use the original counts in the calculation. Rounding the two individual odds to 0.018 and 0.003 before dividing would obscure the difference between the odds ratio and the risk ratio.



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#disease-or-with-10-of-controls

title: Case-Control Studies

Disease OR With 10% of Controls

Sample odds with severe hypertension = 180 / 982 ≈ 0.1833
Sample odds with normal blood pressure = 30 / 997 ≈ 0.03009
Disease OR = (180 / 982) / (30 / 997) ≈ 6.09

Participants with severe hypertension had 6.09 times the odds of MI over one year compared with normotensive participants. The individual sample odds differ from the population odds.



We can repeat the calculation using the 10% sample of controls. Both row odds are ten times the corresponding cohort odds, so their ratio is unchanged.
These individual sample odds do not estimate the population odds of MI directly. The odds ratio is preserved because we sampled the same fraction of exposed and unexposed non-cases while retaining all cases.
With appropriate control sampling, the odds ratio estimates the disease odds ratio in the source population. When the outcome is rare, it can also approximate the risk ratio.
Random samples will introduce sampling error. This example keeps the exposure proportions exactly constant to show the underlying calculation.



Source: Szklo and Nieto, Epidemiology. Jones & Bartlett Learning.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#interpreting-the-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#interpreting-the-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Interpreting the Odds Ratio

Interpreting the Odds Ratio (OR)

OR = 1: No association between exposure and disease
OR > 1: Exposure is associated with higher odds of disease
OR < 1: Exposure is associated with lower odds of disease

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#strengths-and-limitations
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#strengths-and-limitations
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Strengths and Limitations


Strengths

Efficient for studying rare diseases
Faster and less costly than cohort studies
Require fewer participants
Useful for diseases with long latency


Limitations

Cannot directly measure incidence or risk
Vulnerable to selection bias
Prone to recall bias
Control selection can be challenging

Cohort vs. Case-Control Studies



Feature
Cohort Study
Case-Control Study




Start With
Exposure
Outcome


Direction
Exposure → Outcome
Outcome → Exposure


Measure
Relative Risk (RR)
Odds Ratio (OR)


Best For

Rare diseases

Longer, more expensive

Yes

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-sampling
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-sampling
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Sampling
In a case-control study, we typically sample based on the _____ we are interested in studying.
A. Exposure
B. Outcome

In a case-control study, we typically start with an outcome we are interested in studying. We then sample (select) people for the study based on the presence or absence of that outcome.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Identify the Study Design
Researchers survey 1,000 adults at a single point in time, asking about their current smoking status and whether they currently have a chronic cough. What type of study is this?
A. Cohort study
B. Case-control study
C. Cross-sectional study
D. Randomized trial

Answer: Cross-sectional study. Smoking status and cough are assessed at the same time.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design-1
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design-1
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Identify the Study Design
Researchers use medical records from 2010 to identify 1,000 smokers and 1,000 nonsmokers who were free of lung cancer. They review records through 2020 to determine who developed lung cancer. All records already exist when the study begins. What type of study is this?
A. Cohort study
B. Case-control study
C. Cross-sectional study
D. Randomized trial

Answer: Retrospective cohort study. Researchers group people by past exposure and use existing records to compare subsequent disease occurrence.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design-2
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identify-the-study-design-2
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Identify the Study Design
Researchers sample 500 patients who have lung cancer and 500 patients who do not have lung cancer. They compare the two groups’ smoking histories before the lung cancer diagnoses. What type of study is this?
A. Cohort study
B. Case-control study
C. Cross-sectional study
D. Randomized trial

Answer: Case-control study. Participants are selected based on disease status, and researchers compare their prior exposure.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-study-base-principle
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-study-base-principle
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Study Base Principle
Shands Hospital at the University of Florida is a referral hospital for a variety of cancer diagnoses -- including bronchogenic carcinoma -- for the North Florida region where it is located. 
Researchers are interested in the association between bronchogenic carcinoma and a history of cigarette smoking, and they decide to conduct a case-control study. Cases are selected from the admissions records to the cancer center. Controls are randomly selected from the population of the surrounding county.
Does the control group violate the study base principle?
A. Probably
B. Probably not

Remember that the study base principle tells us that cases and controls should be “representative of the same base experience.” One way to conceptualize this in our heads is to think of the study base as those who would have been selected as cases if they developed the disease. Based on the narrative above, it seems like people from the surrounding county would likely go to Shands if they developed bronchogenic carcinoma, and then they would have had the same probability of selection as any other case. Therefore, the study base principle is probably not violated in this scenario.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-control-selection
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-control-selection
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Control Selection
Researchers are interested in the effect of obesity on colorectal cancer and conduct a case-control study. Cases are selected from a large colon cancer registry. Researchers are concerned that unmeasured genetic factors may bias study results.
What would be a good control group to remove the potential confounding effects of genetic factors?

Matching study subjects with siblings may be used in both cohort and case-control studies to control for shared genetic and environmental factors. (Modern Epidemiology, 4th ed.)

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identifying-bias
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-identifying-bias
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Identifying Bias
In a case-control study investigating the relationship between alcohol use and liver cancer, cases were recruited from a major urban hospital. Controls were recruited from a local fitness club.
Which bias is most likely?
A. Recall bias
B. Attrition bias
C. Selection bias
D. Interviewer bias

Explanation: Controls from a fitness club may not represent the same source population as hospital cases, leading to distorted exposure comparison.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-odds
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-odds
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Interpreting Odds
In a study of Parkinson’s disease, the odds of prior pesticide exposure among cases were 0.25, or 1 to 4.
What does this mean?
A. 25% of cases had prior pesticide exposure
B. For every 1 case with prior pesticide exposure, there were 4 cases without prior exposure
C. Cases had 25% greater risk of pesticide exposure
D. Cases were 4 times as likely to have prior pesticide exposure as to have no prior exposure

Correct answer: B.
Odds of 1 to 4 mean 1 exposed case for every 4 unexposed cases. The corresponding proportion exposed is 1 / (1 + 4) = 20%, not 25%.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-an-odds-ratio
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-an-odds-ratio
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Interpreting an Odds Ratio
In a case-control study, researchers compared patients with Parkinson’s disease to controls without Parkinson’s disease. The odds ratio for prior pesticide exposure was 2.5.
What does this mean?
A. Pesticide exposure causes Parkinson’s disease
B. People exposed to pesticides had 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
C. Parkinson’s disease cases had 2.5 times the odds of prior pesticide exposure compared to controls
D. 2.5% of Parkinson’s disease cases had prior pesticide exposure

Correct answer: C.
An OR greater than 1 indicates a positive association. Cases had higher odds of prior exposure than controls. This result does not directly measure risk or establish causation.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-an-odds-ratio-1
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Case-Control Studies/Case-Control Studies.html#practice-interpreting-an-odds-ratio-1
title: Case-Control Studies
text:
Practice: Interpreting an Odds Ratio
In a case-control study, researchers compared patients with Alzheimer’s disease to controls without Alzheimer’s disease. The odds ratio for regular physical activity during midlife was 0.60.
What does this mean?
A. Alzheimer’s disease cases had 40% lower odds of regular physical activity during midlife compared to controls
B. Physically active people had 60% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease
C. Regular physical activity prevents Alzheimer’s disease
D. There was no association between physical activity and Alzheimer’s disease

Correct answer: A.
Cases had 0.60 times the odds of prior regular physical activity compared to controls. This is equivalent to 40% lower odds: (1 − 0.60) × 100%.
An OR less than 1 indicates an inverse association. This result does not establish that physical activity prevents Alzheimer’s disease.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#epidemiological-study-fundamental-question
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#epidemiological-study-fundamental-question
title: Association and Causality
text:
Epidemiological Study: Fundamental Question
After identifying patterns (Person–Place–Time), we ask:

Are exposure and outcome linked?
Is the observed association valid or misleading?
Could chance, bias, or confounding explain the finding?
Does the evidence support a causal interpretation?



Last week, we discussed descriptive epidemiology - describing the occurrence of exposures and outcomes - but we are rarely content to stop there.
We’ll discuss each of these terms a little bit today.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#disease-causality-concepts-over-time
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#disease-causality-concepts-over-time
title: Association and Causality
text:
Disease Causality: Concepts Over Time
Causal explanations evolve with available evidence, tools, and methods.

Supernatural explanations: Disease attributed to fate, spirits, or moral forces
Environmental (Miasma) theories: Illness linked to air, water, climate, and surroundings
Germ theory: Specific biological agents identified as causes of many infectious diseases
Risk-factor & multicausal models: Most diseases arise from multiple interacting factors, not a single cause
Modern epidemiology: Causal inference integrates biology, behavior, environment, and social context over time

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#what-do-epidemiologists-report-first
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#what-do-epidemiologists-report-first
title: Association and Causality
text:
What Do Epidemiologists Report First?

When studying health in populations, epidemiologists usually start by reporting:
A. Clear cause-and-effect relationships
B. Patterns and correlations
C. Biological mechanisms
D. Random events with no structure


We usually report patterns and correlations first.
Causality requires additional evaluation and assumptions.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#association
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#association
title: Association and Causality
text:
Association

Association: The distribution of an outcome differs across levels of an exposure.

For example, the outcome may be more common in one group than another.

Knowing something about X helps us predict something about Y.
Types: Positive association and negative association.
An association alone does not tell us why the groups differ.



The outcome’s distribution can differ in its average, spread, or proportion in each category.
An association does not require a statistically significant p-value. Evaluating random error is a separate question.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#types-of-association
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#types-of-association
title: Association and Causality
text:
Types of Association


Positive Association

Negative Association

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Causality

Causality: A relationship where a change in one factor directly produces a change in an outcome.
Key distinctions

Causality implies association
Association does not imply causality

Why causality is harder to establish

Multiple contributing factors
Role of chance, bias, and confounding
Ethical and practical limits on experimentation




Another way to think about the distinction: If I changed X and held everything else constant, would I expect Y to change?

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#the-search-for-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#the-search-for-causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
The Search for Causality

When an association is observed, epidemiologists may ask:

Is the association causal?
Could chance, bias, or confounding explain it?
Is the association consistent with what we (think we) know about how the world works?
Across time, place, populations, and biology?
Does the evidence support a causal interpretation?
Or are alternative explanations more plausible?

Key idea: Causality is not proven by a single study, but evaluated through accumulated evidence.



We are rarely content to stop at description or even prediction.
We will talk about chance, bias, and confounding next.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#bias
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#bias
title: Association and Causality
text:
Bias

Bias: Systematic error in an estimate. The gap between what we measured and what we intended to measure.
Bias can arise from who enters a study, how we measure variables, or how we estimate a causal effect.



Example: We want to estimate average physical activity among all Texas adults, so we measure physical activity patterns at local gyms.




Key idea: A larger sample does not generally eliminate bias.




Our sample will likely systematically overrepresent more active people.
Because the error is systematic, a larger sample will not generally eliminate the bias.
Transition to the next slide: Confounding is one source of bias when estimating causal effects. Some epidemiology texts distinguish confounding from other biases; for today, emphasize how each can lead our estimate away from the quantity we want to understand.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#confounding
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#confounding
title: Association and Causality
text:
Confounding

Confounding: The effects of other factors become mixed into our estimate of an exposure’s causal effect. Or giving credit to the wrong variable.
Example: Ice cream sales and drownings both increase during hot weather.

Hot weather influences both ice cream sales and drowning risk.

Question: Would reducing ice cream sales reduce drownings?
Key idea: The association can be real and useful for prediction without representing a causal effect of ice cream sales.


The association itself need not be incorrect. The problem arises when we attribute it to a causal effect of ice cream sales rather than the common cause, hot weather.
Introduce the term “spurious association” here for the reading, quiz, and later exercise. It describes an association that does not represent the causal relationship we might infer from it. Do not use it as a synonym for confounding: chance and other biases can also produce misleading findings.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-sunscreen-use-and-skin-cancer
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-sunscreen-use-and-skin-cancer
title: Association and Causality
section: Exercise: Sunscreen Use and Skin Cancer
text:
Exercise: Sunscreen Use and Skin Cancer

Observed association: Higher rates of skin cancer are associated with increased sunscreen use.
Question: What might confound the relationship between sunscreen use and skin cancer?
Think about:

Who is more likely to use sunscreen?
What other exposure might be related to both sunscreen use and skin cancer?



Answer: Sun exposure is a potential confounder. People who spend more time in the sun may be more likely to use sunscreen, and greater sun exposure also increases skin cancer risk. The observed association alone does not establish that sunscreen causes skin cancer.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-which-is-a-spurious-association
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-which-is-a-spurious-association
title: Association and Causality
section: Exercise: Which Is a Spurious Association?
text:
Exercise: Which Is a Spurious Association?
Which scenario shows a spurious association?
A. As outside temperature drops, more people wear hats.
B. As vaccination rates increase, the targeted disease decreases.
C. Fires attended by more firefighters tend to cause more property damage.
D. People who exercise regularly have lower rates of heart disease.

A. As outside temperature drops, more people wear hats. This is not spurious. Cold temperature plausibly causes both discomfort and hat use. This is a reasonable causal relationship, not a misleading one.
B. As MMR vaccination rates increase, measles incidence decreases. This is a plausible causal association supported by strong evidence. Students may say “this is still just an association,” which is technically true, but it is not spurious because no third factor explains both in opposite directions. Extensive experimental and observational evidence supports causality.
C. Fires attended by more firefighters tend to cause more property damage. ✅ Classic spurious association.
D. People who exercise regularly have lower rates of heart disease. This is an association that may be causal but is not obviously spurious. Students may argue confounding (diet, SES), which is valid.
Notice that these are population averages. Not every person wears a hat when the temperature drops outside.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#population-sample-uncertainty
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#population-sample-uncertainty
title: Association and Causality
text:
Population, Sample & Uncertainty
Example: We want to understand the health of adults living in Texas.








Group
Who belongs to it?
In our example




Target population
People we want findings to apply to
All Texas adults


Source population
People from whom we select participants
Adult patients at several Texas clinics


Study sample
People whose data we analyze
500 participating patients





Chance: Would another random sample from the same source give a different estimate?
Applicability: How well do these findings apply to all Texas adults?



Sampling introduces uncertainty into our estimates. Who we recruit also affects which populations our findings may apply to. These are distinct questions: a larger clinic sample does not automatically make it representative of all Texas adults.
Distinguish statistical uncertainty from causal uncertainty, as in Measures of Occurrence, slides 14–16. Even a precisely estimated association can leave uncertainty about its causal interpretation.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#role-of-chance-in-associationcausality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#role-of-chance-in-associationcausality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Role of Chance in Association/Causality
Sampling variability: Estimates differ from sample to sample, even when we sample randomly from the same population.




Hypothetical BMI example

Population mean: 28
One random sample: 30
Another random sample might have a mean of 26.

Question: Must a difference between an estimate and the truth mean someone made a mistake?


Answer: No. Samples can differ by chance. In practice, we usually do not know the true population mean. The same idea applies to estimates of associations: sampling variability can exaggerate, weaken, or reverse an observed association.
Sampling variability is one source of random error. The old deck also illustrates random measurement error. Random error need not average to exactly zero across a small number of samples.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#controlling-for-chance-in-epidemiologic-studies
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#controlling-for-chance-in-epidemiologic-studies
title: Association and Causality
section: Controlling for Chance in Epidemiologic Studies
text:
Controlling for Chance in Epidemiologic Studies

Larger samples generally reduce sampling variability.
Systematic bias is a different problem. A larger sample does not typically correct biased recruitment, measurement, or confounding.
Precision and causality are different questions. We can estimate an association precisely and still be uncertain whether it is causal.
Key idea: More data can improve precision, but causal interpretation still requires careful judgment.


Increasing sample size generally reduces sampling variability when other features of the study are comparable. It does not guarantee that a particular estimate is closer to the truth. Comparing exposed and unexposed groups is essential to many association questions, but doing so alone does not control chance.
Now, we will transition from association to causation…

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#types-of-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#types-of-causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Types of Causality

Deterministic causality

A cause leads to an outcome with certainty
If the cause occurs, the outcome follows
Everyday example: Pressing a light switch → the light turns on

Probabilistic causality

A cause changes the chance of an outcome
The outcome does not always occur
Everyday example: Studying more → higher chance of doing well on an exam
Epidemiology focuses mostly on probabilistic causality.




Can we really even call the light switch example completely deterministic? Does the light ALWAYS come on when we press the light switch?
Ask what else must be present: electricity, a working bulb, and a complete circuit. Return to these conditions when introducing component causes.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#deterministic-causality-in-epidemiology-rare
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#deterministic-causality-in-epidemiology-rare
title: Association and Causality
text:
Deterministic Causality in Epidemiology (Rare)

Defining feature: Exposure leads to disease with near certainty
Why it’s unusual

Most diseases involve multiple interacting causes
Individual susceptibility and context matter

Epidemiologic example

Untreated rabies virus exposure → rabies disease

Key takeaway: Deterministic causality exists in epidemiology, but it is rare and exceptional.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#probabilistic-causality-in-epidemiology-typical
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#probabilistic-causality-in-epidemiology-typical
title: Association and Causality
text:
Probabilistic Causality in Epidemiology (Typical)

Defining feature: Exposure increases the likelihood of disease
Why this is typical

Diseases arise from multiple interacting causes
Susceptibility varies across individuals

Epidemiologic example

Smoking → higher risk of lung cancer

Key takeaway: Most epidemiologic causal relationships involve risk, not certainty.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-which-best-describes-deterministic-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#exercise-which-best-describes-deterministic-causality
title: Association and Causality
section: Exercise: Which Best Describes Deterministic Causality?
text:
Exercise: Which Best Describes Deterministic Causality?
Which example best fits deterministic causality?
A. A medication leads to different levels of improvement across patients
B. A specific bacterium always causes disease in people without immunity
C. Increased exercise in a population is linked to lower heart disease rates
D. Rising global temperature is correlated with rising sea levels

Explanation: Deterministic causality implies a fixed, predictable, and consistent cause-and-effect relationship. If a certain cause is present, the effect will always occur. In option B, the presence of a specific pathogen leading to disease in susceptible individuals is an example of a deterministic cause-and-effect scenario, assuming no other factors, such as immunity, intervene.
Brad’s notes I left this in here in case it’s on the quiz. However, I’d try to train myself to think about it this way: - Virtually no outcome is truly deterministic.
- If a particular exposure-outcome relationship happens to be pretty close to deterministic, how can we use that to our advantage?

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#multivariate-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#multivariate-causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Multivariate Causality

Most health outcomes involve multiple contributing causes.
Causes can act together, and different combinations can produce the same outcome.

Return to the light switch: What else must be present for flipping the switch to turn on the light?


Electricity, a working bulb, and a complete circuit.
Flipping the switch may complete the combination of conditions needed for the light to turn on.

Key idea: The final event in a sequence is not necessarily the only cause.


Pause for students to name the other conditions before revealing or discussing the examples. Use this as the transition to Rothman’s model: a component contributes to a causal mechanism, while a complete set is sufficient to produce the outcome.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#rothmans-model-of-sufficient-and-component-causes-rmscc
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#rothmans-model-of-sufficient-and-component-causes-rmscc
title: Association and Causality
section: Rothman’s Model of Sufficient and Component Causes (RMSCC)
text:
Rothman’s Model of Sufficient and Component Causes (RMSCC)




Outcome: Flu

Each pie is a sufficient cause set - “sufficient” to produce the outcome
Each slice represents a component cause
Different combinations of slices can produce the same outcome
A necessary cause is a component cause that appears in every sufficient cause set



? = unknown causes. These pies illustrate hypothetical causal mechanisms.
Connect this to the light-switch example: the switch, electricity, bulb, and circuit contribute to a complete causal mechanism. We often notice the last component, but the other components also matter.
Work through examples. Make sure to discuss necessary and sufficient causes.
Key takeaway: Disease occurs when enough causes act together, not from one cause alone.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#quick-review-association-vs-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#quick-review-association-vs-causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Quick Review: Association vs Causality
What distinguishes a causal relationship from an association?
A. A causal relationship means the two factors increase at the same time.
B. A causal relationship means changes in one factor lead to changes in another, with evidence that the exposure occurs before the outcome.
C. An association requires a statistically significant p-value, while a causal relationship does not.
D. Associations can only be observed in laboratory settings, while causal relationships are observed in real-world settings.

Causality implies that there is a direct cause-and-effect link between two variables, and it is established through various criteria such as temporality (cause precedes effect), strength (strong association), consistency (repeated observations across studies), plausibility (biological rationale), and others. An association may suggest that two variables are related in some way, but it does not confirm that one causes the other.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#hills-viewpoints-for-causality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#hills-viewpoints-for-causality
title: Association and Causality
text:
Hill’s Viewpoints for Causality

Context: Proposed by Sir Austin Bradford Hill (1965) to guide causal reasoning in epidemiology
Purpose: A set of nine principles to consider when evaluating whether an observed association is likely to be causal
Important clarifications

Not a checklist
Not all criteria must be met
Temporality (exposure precedes outcome) is essential

Key idea: Hill’s guidelines organize evidence; they do not prove causation.



Well, a perfectly natural human thing to do is to make a checklist and start to classify things based on that checklist.
One famous example of such a checklist, which was never intended by the author to be a checklist, is Hill’s guidelines. Hill’s description was “nine different viewpoints from all of which we should study association before we cry causation.”
Your assigned readings covered Hill’s guidelines and why these guidelines are absolutely not sufficient for distinguishing causal from non-causal associations.
However, they still have historical significance in the sense that these criteria, along with a lot of observational data, resulted in consensus that smoking was an important cause of lung cancer. Not merely associated with lung cancer.
I think it can also be instructive to review the ways in which each of these guidelines, as intuitive as they may seem, cannot be relied upon for drawing causal conclusions.
Having said that, you do feel better about your results when they conform to some, or all, of these guidelines.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#strength-of-association-effect-size
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#strength-of-association-effect-size
title: Association and Causality
text:
1. Strength of Association (Effect Size)
A small association does not mean that there is not a causal effect, though the larger the association, the more likely that it is causal.

Example: People who smoke cigarettes are about 25 times as likely to develop lung cancer as people who do not smoke (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2014).
Limitations: Strong associations can still arise from confounding or bias. Effect size alone does not establish causation.
Counterexample: Children’s shoe sizes and reading aptitude are associated. What could explain both?



Would a risk ratio of 25 make you more confident in a causal explanation than a risk ratio of 1.2? Why?
Increasing shoe size would not itself improve reading.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#consistency-reproducibility
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#consistency-reproducibility
title: Association and Causality
text:
2. Consistency (Reproducibility)
Consistent findings across studies, populations, and settings strengthen the likelihood of a causal effect.

Example: Higher sodium intake is associated with higher blood pressure across populations in many countries (Elliott et al. 1996).
Limitation: Studies that share the same bias can produce consistently misleading findings.
Counterexample: Suppose studies in many cities consistently find that ice cream sales and murders rise together. Does repeating this finding mean that ice cream causes murder?



If we repeated the ice cream and murder study many times, what do you think we would find?
Seasonal factors could affect both ice cream sales and violence. If every study fails to account for those factors, the same misleading association could appear repeatedly. Replication does not automatically eliminate confounding.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#specificity
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#specificity
title: Association and Causality
text:
3. Specificity
An association concentrated in a particular exposure–disease relationship can support a causal interpretation, but specificity is not required.

Example: A disease-causing expansion of CAG (cytosine–adenine–guanine) repeats in the HTT gene causes Huntington’s disease—a specific genetic alteration linked to a particular disease (National Library of Medicine 2020).
Limitations: One exposure can cause several diseases, and one disease can have several causes. A lack of specificity does not rule out causation.
Counterexample: Does the fact that smoking causes lung cancer make it any less likely that it also causes heart disease?



Specificity concerns which disease is linked to a cause, not whether everyone with the cause develops disease. People with 36–39 CAG repeats may or may not develop Huntington’s disease; people with 40 or more repeats almost always develop it (National Library of Medicine 2020).
This criterion is less emphasized today because many exposures have multiple effects.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#temporality
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#temporality
title: Association and Causality
text:
4. Temporality
The effect has to occur after the cause (and if there is an expected delay between the cause and expected effect, then the effect must occur after that delay).

Example: Smoking precedes lung cancer development.
Limitations: The order of exposure and outcome may be difficult to establish. Even when an exposure clearly precedes an outcome, that sequence alone does not mean it caused the outcome.
Counterexample: A rooster crows before sunrise. Does it cause sunrise?
Key idea: Temporality is necessary, but timing alone does not establish causality.



The rooster example shows why occurring first is not sufficient.
Question: Generally speaking, can we establish temporality in case reports and cross-sectional studies?

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#biological-gradient-dose-response
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#biological-gradient-dose-response
title: Association and Causality
text:
5. Biological Gradient (Dose-Response)
Increasing exposure is associated with increasing risk of the outcome, which can support a causal interpretation.

Example: Smoking more cigarettes per day is associated with higher lung cancer risk.
Limitations: Threshold effects and nonlinear relationships.
Counterexample: Suppose days with higher ice cream sales also have more drownings. Does buying more ice cream increase the risk of drowning?



Hot weather could increase both ice cream sales and swimming. The resulting gradient could reflect confounding by temperature rather than a causal effect of ice cream.
A graded association can occur without causation. Threshold effects and nonlinear relationships illustrate the other direction: a causal relationship may exist without a simple increasing gradient.
Threshold effect: Vitamin C deficiency and scurvy: Scurvy can develop after many weeks of extremely low vitamin C intake. The threshold varies with body stores and duration of deficiency.

Disease may appear only after exposure—here, deprivation—passes a critical level.

Diminishing returns: Physical activity and mortality: Moving from inactivity to some activity is associated with substantial reductions in mortality risk; additional activity provides progressively smaller reductions.

Equal increases in exposure do not necessarily produce equal changes in risk.

U-shaped relationship: iodine and thyroid dysfunction: Both too little and too much iodine can cause thyroid problems, including hypothyroidism.

Risk can be higher at both low and high exposure levels.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#biological-plausibility
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#biological-plausibility
title: Association and Causality
text:
6. Biological Plausibility
A plausible mechanism between cause and effect increases the likelihood of a causal effect.

Example: Chemicals in tobacco smoke can damage DNA in lung cells. That damage can disrupt the control of cell growth and lead to cancer (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2024).
Limitation: What seems biologically plausible depends on current knowledge. A convincing explanation can be wrong, and a real causal effect may exist before its mechanism is understood.
Counterexample: Miasma theory of disease causation.


The mechanism can be summarized as: tobacco smoke → DNA damage → uncontrolled cell growth → cancer.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#coherence
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#coherence
title: Association and Causality
text:
7. Coherence
Coherence between epidemiological and laboratory findings increases the likelihood of a causal effect.

Example: Smoking-related lung cancer aligns with known carcinogenic effects of tobacco.
Limitations: Agreement with existing knowledge does not rule out alternative explanations. Apparent disagreement may reflect gaps or errors in current knowledge rather than the absence of a causal effect.
Counterexample:

Epidemiology: Observational studies found lower coronary heart disease risk among hormone users (Grodstein et al. 1996).
Biology: Hormone therapy lowered LDL cholesterol, supporting a possible protective mechanism (The Writing Group for the PEPI Trial 1995).
Later evidence: The Women’s Health Initiative randomized trial found that the estrogen-plus-progestin regimen tested did not prevent coronary heart disease and could increase its risk (Manson et al. 2003).

Comparison: Consistency compares studies. Coherence compares findings with existing knowledge.



Coherence asks whether the evidence fits together, but fitting together does not guarantee that our explanation is correct. Conversely, we should not dismiss a finding simply because laboratory evidence is missing. Hill explicitly cautioned that a lack of laboratory support cannot invalidate epidemiological observations.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#experiment
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#experiment
title: Association and Causality
text:
8. Experiment
Well-designed randomized experiments can strengthen causal inference by changing exposure and reducing confounding.

Example: In the DASH-Sodium trial, participants consumed diets with different sodium levels in random order. Lower sodium intake reduced blood pressure (Sacks et al. 2001).
Limitations: Experiments may be unethical or impractical. Missing outcomes, poor adherence, and measurement problems can undermine results. Findings may not generalize beyond the participants and conditions studied.
Counterexample: Suppose a randomized treatment trial loses follow-up data from participants whose health worsens. Could the treatment appear more effective than it really is?



Randomization helps make groups comparable at the start, but it does not prevent every problem afterward. If missing outcomes are related to treatment and health, analyzing only participants with complete data can produce a misleading result.
Experimental evidence is also not required to establish causation: we do not need to assign people to start smoking to determine that smoking causes disease.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#analogy
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#analogy
title: Association and Causality
text:
9. Analogy
A known causal relationship can suggest that a similar exposure might produce a similar outcome.

Example: Rubella infection during pregnancy can cause birth defects. By analogy, another viral infection during pregnancy—such as Zika—might also harm fetal development (Rasmussen et al. 2016).
Limitations: Similarities may be superficial. Similar exposures can act through different mechanisms and produce different outcomes. Analogy suggests a hypothesis; it does not establish causation.
Counterexample: Smoking and getting punched in the gut can both make someone cough. Does that mean both cause lung cancer?



The relevant similarity in the example is maternal infection with the potential to affect fetal development. Evidence specific to Zika was still needed.
The counterexample illustrates a weak analogy: sharing one consequence—coughing—does not mean two exposures share other consequences.

Coherence: Does this explanation fit the broader evidence?
Analogy: Does this resemble another known cause-and-effect relationship?

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#best-practices-for-thinking-about-hills-viewpoints
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#best-practices-for-thinking-about-hills-viewpoints
title: Association and Causality
section: Best Practices for Thinking About Hill’s Viewpoints
text:
Best Practices for Thinking About Hill’s Viewpoints

Start with temporality: If exposure does not precede outcome, causality cannot be established.
Evaluate criteria collectively: No single criterion is sufficient. Temporality is necessary, but it is not sufficient.
Consider alternative explanations: Always assess confounding, bias, and chance.
Avoid checklist thinking: Hill’s viewpoints guide reasoning but do not prove causation.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#the-search-for-causality-evali-outbreak-example
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#the-search-for-causality-evali-outbreak-example
title: Association and Causality
section: The Search for Causality: EVALI Outbreak Example
text:
The Search for Causality: EVALI Outbreak Example

EVALI: E-cigarette or Vaping–Associated Lung Injury
Question: How did epidemiologists move from observation to causal judgment?

Observation (Early 2019): Surge in lung injuries among people who reported vaping
Initial hypotheses: Vaping products may be linked to lung injury: Which products? Which components?
Data collection (Mid-2019): Patient histories, product testing, pattern comparison
Evidence accumulation (Late 2019): Vitamin E acetate identified in many THC-containing products
Causal inference (2020): Evidence supports a causal role for vitamin E acetate in EVALI


Vitamin E acetate is a thick, sticky substance added to some vaping products and can be harmful when inhaled, unlike regular vitamin E, which is a nutrient found in foods that’s good for your skin and overall health.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#example-zika-virus-microcephaly
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#example-zika-virus-microcephaly
title: Association and Causality
text:
Example: Zika Virus & Microcephaly



Zika virus is a member of the virus family Flaviviridae. It is spread by daytime-active Aedes mosquitoes.
Microcephaly is a medical condition involving a smaller-than-normal head.






The Zika virus is a disease that you can get from mosquito bites in certain parts of the world. If a pregnant woman gets bitten by a mosquito carrying Zika, there’s a chance it can harm her unborn baby. One serious problem it can cause is microcephaly, where the baby’s head and brain don’t develop properly and are smaller than they should be. This can lead to serious health and development issues for the baby as it grows.


(Kuadkitkan et al. 2020)

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#group-activity-zika-virus-and-causal-reasoning
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#group-activity-zika-virus-and-causal-reasoning
title: Association and Causality
section: Group Activity: Zika Virus and Causal Reasoning
text:
Group Activity: Zika Virus and Causal Reasoning



You will watch a short video about the Zika virus and microcephaly.
Each group has been assigned a different lens for evaluating causality at this Google link: https://tinyurl.com/W5GroupActivity or via the QR code
While watching the video:

Focus only on your assigned lens and the last slide about dose-response 
Capture brief bullet points, not full sentences

After the video, your group should report:

One piece of evidence that supports causality
One limitation or uncertainty related to your lens

As a whole class, we will then discuss:

Whether there is evidence of a dose–response relationship, and
Why some causal criteria may be harder to demonstrate than others






Instructions
- Assign groups 1-8.
- Ask them to scan the QR code and read the slide for their group before we watch the video.

href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#video-zika-virus-microcephaly
title: Association and Causality
text:
Video: Zika Virus & Microcephaly


“As you watch, listen for which pieces of evidence strengthened the causal argument and which questions remained.”

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#causality-criteria-zika-virus-microcephaly
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#causality-criteria-zika-virus-microcephaly
title: Association and Causality
text:
Causality Criteria: Zika Virus & Microcephaly

Temporality: Pregnant mothers got Zika before having babies with microcephaly.
Strength: Big spike in microcephaly where Zika outbreaks occurred.
Consistency: Similar rises reported in multiple regions (e.g., Brazil, French Polynesia).
Specificity: Most increases appeared where Zika was active (though microcephaly has other causes).
Dose-Response (Biological Gradient): More severe or earlier Zika infections may lead to higher risk of microcephaly.
Biological Plausibility: Zika infects developing brain cells, a direct biological link to smaller head size.
Coherence: Fits with existing knowledge that viruses can damage fetal brain development.
Experiment: No direct clinical trials (ethical limits), but strong observational and lab evidence.
Analogy: Similar viruses (e.g., rubella) cause birth defects, supporting the Zika-microcephaly link.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#putting-it-all-together
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#putting-it-all-together
title: Association and Causality
text:
Putting It All Together

Causal inference in epidemiology requires careful judgment.

Associations are typically reported first.
Causality is evaluated using multiple lines of evidence.
Most diseases have multiple contributing causes.
Uncertainty and chance are always present.

Final takeaway: Epidemiology is about making the best possible causal judgments with imperfect evidence.

objectID: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#references
href: Module 05 - Association and Causality/Association and Causality/Association and Causality.html#references
title: Association and Causality
text:

title: Disease Occurrence Data
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you should be able to:

Identify key factors that influence epidemiologic data quality.
Distinguish between vital statistics and reportable/notifiable disease data.
Identify major surveillance programs in the United States.
Describe major sources of epidemiologic data used in public health.



In our last module we learned about calculating some foundational epidemiologic measures.
Ask the class to recall some examples of measures of event/disease/outcome occurrence that are commonly used in epidemiology.
But where do we get the data to calculate those measures? That’s today’s topic.
Before diving in, let’s complete a reading comprehension exercise to refresh your memory and solidify what you read for this week.

What does data linkage mean?


A. Removing identifying information from a database.
B. Summarizing records within a single database.
C. Joining information from databases using a common identifier.

Respond here

B: Keep going. Summarizing records describes information already in a database. Linkage joins information across databases.

Reading Comprehension Quiz 02


What is the main purpose of data mining?


A. Finding previously unrecognized patterns in large amounts of data.
B. Proving that every observed relationship is a cause of disease.
C. Replacing electronic records with printed copies of the same information.
D. Removing every error from a collection of health records.


Respond here



Answer: A. A: That’s right. Data mining explores large amounts of data to help us discover patterns and associations.
B: Good effort. A pattern can show an association, but data mining alone does not establish that one factor causes another.
C: Keep going. Changing how records are stored is different from exploring their contents for patterns.

Reading Comprehension Quiz 03


How do census data help us calculate population-based disease rates?


A. They identify the immediate cause of each recorded death.
B. They confirm the diagnosis of each reported disease case.
C. They describe the treatment received by each hospital patient.
D. They provide population counts for the denominator of a rate.

B: Keep going. Census data describe populations; they do not confirm individual disease diagnoses.

What limitation of death certificate data does the chapter describe?

Reading Comprehension Quiz 05


What is the main purpose of public health surveillance?


A. Continuously collecting, analyzing, and sharing health information to guide public health action.
B. Providing individual treatment plans during routine appointments with healthcare providers.
C. Collecting health information once and storing it without analysis or interpretation.
D. Assigning participants to treatments to compare the effects of different medicines.


Respond here



Answer: A. A: That’s right. Surveillance helps us monitor health problems over time and share findings that support public health action.
B: Good effort. Individual treatment is part of clinical care. Surveillance gathers and uses information about health in populations.
C: Keep going. Surveillance is ongoing and includes analyzing, interpreting, and sharing information, not just storing it.
D: Good effort. Assigning treatments is part of an experimental study. Surveillance monitors the occurrence of health problems and risk factors. Reveal the answer: after_discussion. If polling fails: Read the question aloud, allow time for us to think, then take a show of hands for each option and discuss the answers together.

What makes a disease a reportable disease?


A. Its cases are described in a published research article.
B. Its cases are counted in the population census.
