objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpreting-the-baseline-table
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpreting-the-baseline-table
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Interpreting the Baseline Table

Ratios close to 1 indicate similar proportions with these measured baseline characteristics.

These rows contain baseline comparisons, so they describe participants before treatment.

Similarity in these measured characteristics does not establish similarity in every measured or unmeasured characteristic.

Randomization supports comparability on average; chance differences can remain in a particular trial.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#internal-and-external-validity
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#internal-and-external-validity
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Internal and External Validity

Internal validity: Does the study provide an unbiased estimate of the association among the people studied?

Comparable groups at baseline, like the aspirin and placebo groups we just examined, support internal validity.

External validity: Do the findings apply to people outside the study?

This depends on who enrolled. Would the aspirin results hold for people who differ from the trial participants in age, sex, or health?




The baseline table answered a question about what happened inside the trial: were the aspirin and placebo groups comparable? That’s a question about internal validity, meaning whether the trial gives an unbiased answer for the people in it.
A separate question is whether that answer carries over to the people we actually want to treat. That’s external validity. Randomization doesn’t help with this one, because it depends on who enrolled in the trial, not on how they were assigned to groups.
Keep these two questions in mind on the next slide. RCTs tend to be strong on the first and weaker on the second.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#rcts-strengths-limitations
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#rcts-strengths-limitations
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
RCTs: Strengths & Limitations


Strengths

Randomization improves group comparability
Strong internal validity
Typically provides strongest evidence for the causal effects of interventions


Limitations

Often expensive and time-consuming
May have limited generalizability to real-world populations
Not always ethical or feasible



Next, we’ll discuss cohort studies.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#what-is-a-cohort
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#what-is-a-cohort
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
What Is a Cohort?
A cohort is an identified group of people whose membership is defined by a shared characteristic or event.

Example: Everyone who graduated from TCU in 2026.
We can identify who belongs to the group.
In epidemiology, we often follow a cohort over time to observe health outcomes.
Key difference between a population and a cohort: Every member of the cohort is enumerated (i.e., known or listed). That is not necessarily true of a population.



Think of a cohort as a group with a membership rule and a list of people who meet it. The shared event might be graduation, birth during a particular year, or enrollment in a study. Members do not need to know one another or live in the same place.
The graduating class of 2026 is a useful example. Moving away does not change the fact that someone belongs to that graduating class. Similarly, someone who stops responding to a study remains a member of the original enrollment cohort, even though we are no longer observing their outcomes.
A cohort is often the study sample drawn from a larger population. The word describes the group; it does not, by itself, specify the study design. We can follow a cohort in an observational study or a randomized trial. A cohort can also include both exposed and unexposed people.

Source: measures_of_occurrence.pptx, slide 27 and speaker notes; slide cites Lash TL, VanderWeele TJ, Haneuse S, Rothman KJ. Modern Epidemiology. 4th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2021.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#basic-experimental-study-design-1
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#basic-experimental-study-design-1
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Basic Experimental Study Design




We’ve already talked about experimental studies where we start with a cohort of people who have not yet been exposed to our primary exposure of interest and who have not yet experienced our outcome of interest.
For example, if our outcome of interest was the flu and our exposure of interest was the flu vaccine, then our initial source population would only include people who had not yet received the flu vaccine (probably within some window of time) and who didn’t have the flu (probably within some window of time).
We would then choose who gets the flu vaccine and who doesn’t – ideally at random. The study participants do NOT choose their own exposure value.
Next, we follow the cohort of people for some meaningful period of time. When enough time has elapsed, we compare the occurrence of the outcome – in this case the flu – between our exposure groups – in this case, those who did and did not get vaccinated.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Prospective Cohort Study Design



The basic prospective cohort study design is pretty similar to the experimental design we just discussed, with one major difference.
Again, there is some source population out in the world. In that source population, some person or force other than us is choosing whether people are exposed to something we are interested in or not.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-1
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-1
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Prospective Cohort Study Design


Then, we come along and measure how much exposure each person in the cohort has. For this example, there are only two possible levels of exposure: Exposed and unexposed. The orange dots are exposed people and the blue dots are unexposed people.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-2
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-2
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Prospective Cohort Study Design



Now, our goal is to follow these people over some period of time and figure out if exposed people are more likely to get the outcome or if unexposed people are more likely to get the outcome.
That being the case, it wouldn’t make much sense to include people in our cohort who already have the outcome, right?
Therefore, each member of our cohort should be free of the outcome of interest at the beginning of follow-up.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#population-at-risk
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#population-at-risk
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Population at Risk

All members of the cohort should be at risk of developing the outcome of interest.
Implies that all members should be free of the outcome of interest at the outset of follow-up.



Cohorts should consist of people who are at risk of developing the outcome of interest.
This implies that all members of the cohort should be free of the outcome of interest (although they may have other diseases or conditions) at the outset of follow-up.
The reasoning behind this is that someone cannot typically develop a new disease that they already have. Sometimes this criterion is straightforward. Other times, it can be tricky.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-3
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-3
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Prospective Cohort Study Design



Next, we let some time pass and see who develops the outcome and who doesn’t.
We might also say that each time a person gets the outcome, it is an incident occurrence. In this case, each triangle represents an incident.
Further, we can count the number of incidents. For example, there are 6 incident outcomes in the exposed group here.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-4
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-prospective-cohort-study-design-4
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Prospective Cohort Study Design



Finally, after enough time has passed, we will calculate the risk of the outcome in the exposed group, the risk of the outcome in the unexposed group, and compare the two.
As a side note, we are using the word “risk” here colloquially. More specifically, we will typically calculate the incidence proportion in both groups and then compare them as either a ratio of one another or the difference between one another.
And that is the basic prospective cohort study design, also sometimes called a concurrent cohort study design.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-retrospective-cohort-study-design
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#common-retrospective-cohort-study-design
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Common Retrospective Cohort Study Design




Cohort studies can also have a retrospective, or non-concurrent, design.
In a retrospective cohort study, the same sequence of events takes place.
There is some source population out in the world. In that source population, some person or force other than us is choosing whether people are exposed to something we are interested in.
After some time passes, some people will experience the outcome of interest and some won’t.
However, we do not identify the cohort members and start ascertaining measures of exposure and outcome until after people have already started experiencing outcomes. Typically, this is done by reviewing records of some sort.
This is the key distinction between prospective and retrospective cohort studies. In retrospective cohort studies some or all of the outcome incidents have already occurred before we initiate the study.
In contrast, we measure exposures at the initiation of prospective cohort studies before any of the participants have experienced the outcome of interest. The ‘at risk’ period begins after baseline exposure is measured and extends into the future.
In both cases, the measures of exposure and outcome are collected prospectively. The distinction is in who is doing the measuring. In a prospective cohort study, we measure exposures and outcomes.
In a retrospective cohort study, someone else measures the exposures, and typically the outcomes as well. We come along after the fact to gather, match, and analyze those measurements.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#prospective-vs.-retrospective-cohorts
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#prospective-vs.-retrospective-cohorts
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Prospective vs. Retrospective Cohorts

Both follow the same direction: Exposure → Outcome
Both sample on the Exposure
Prospective Cohort

Exposure measured in the present
Outcomes occur in the future

Retrospective Cohort

Exposure and outcome already occurred
Uses existing records
Limited by data quality and missing variables

Key Difference: Timing of data collection — not sampling design.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#when-to-conduct-a-cohort-study
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#when-to-conduct-a-cohort-study
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
section: When to Conduct a Cohort Study
text:
When to Conduct a Cohort Study

Exposure is rare: efficient for studying uncommon exposures
Incidence must be measured: can directly calculate risk and RR
Temporal sequence is important: exposure clearly precedes outcome
Multiple outcomes are of interest: one exposure → several possible diseases
Follow-up is feasible: resources, time, and stable population available
Design Logic: Cohort studies are strongest when you need clear exposure → outcome tracking over time.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#the-framingham-heart-study
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#the-framingham-heart-study
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
The Framingham Heart Study

Study Design: Prospective Cohort Study
What Was Done:

Enrolled 5,209 adults to study the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD)
Measured baseline exposures (e.g., blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking)
Followed participants over time for incident CVD

Why This Design Was Appropriate:

Needed to measure incidence
Required clear exposure → outcome sequence
Allowed one exposure to be linked to multiple outcomes
Long-term follow-up was essential

Key Lesson: Cohort studies are powerful for identifying risk factors over time.



The original cohort included 5,209 adults. The study’s detailed history reports that 5,127 were free of coronary heart disease at baseline. We should not describe all 5,209 participants as disease-free or even as free of all cardiovascular disease.
Participants with existing cardiovascular disease were also followed because one cardiovascular condition could precede another. For example, someone with coronary heart disease could later experience a stroke.
For an analysis of first disease occurrence, the population at risk excludes people who already have that particular outcome. Participants do not need to be free of every disease. Distinguish the full enrolled cohort from the participants eligible for a particular incidence analysis.

Sources: NHLBI study overview; Framingham Heart Study: Epidemiological Background.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#potential-biases-in-cohort-studies
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#potential-biases-in-cohort-studies
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Potential Biases in Cohort Studies

Selection Bias

Loss to follow-up (attrition): selective dropout can cause attrition bias
Example: Participants who developed severe illness were less likely to return for follow-up visits → risk may be underestimated.

Information Bias

Misclassification of exposure
Example: Smoking status or diet self-reported inaccurately at baseline.

Confounding

A third variable related to both exposure and outcome
Example: Age is associated with higher blood pressure and higher CVD risk.

Key Question: Which bias is most important in a long prospective cohort?



This is sort of a trick question, but I decided to leave it.

Any bias is important in any study, regardless of its source.

However, two forms of bias that we tend to be relatively more concerned about in a cohort study than some other study designs include:


Selection bias: A systematic error caused by differences in who enters or remains in the study.

Information bias: A systematic error caused by inaccurate or inconsistent measurement of exposure or outcome.

Why might that be?

Source reminder from Association and Causality: Confounding is one source of bias when estimating causal effects.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#assessing-risk-in-cohort-studies
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#assessing-risk-in-cohort-studies
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Assessing Risk in Cohort Studies

Risk (Incidence Proportion): Number of new cases ÷ population at risk
Relative Risk (RR): Risk in exposed ÷ Risk in unexposed
Absolute Risk Difference (ARD): Risk in exposed − Risk in unexposed
Key Distinction:

RR shows strength of association
ARD shows public health impact

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#a-prospective-cohort-study-example
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#a-prospective-cohort-study-example
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
A Prospective Cohort Study Example

Research Question: Is passive tobacco smoke exposure associated with increased respiratory infections in children?



Study Design:

Enroll disease-free children (<12 years)
Classify by household smoking exposure

Exposed vs Not exposed






Follow forward in time

Measure incident infections





Potential Confounders:

Air pollution
Socioeconomic status
Crowded housing

Next Step: Calculate Risk, RR, and ARD




Research Question: Why can’t we use an RCT to answer this question?

Study Design: So how might we design a study to answer this research question?

Potential Confounders: What are some potential confounding factors we should consider?

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#reading-a-22-table
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#reading-a-22-table
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Reading a 2×2 Table





Infection (+)
Infection (–)
Total




Exposed
A
B
A + B


Not Exposed
C
D
C + D





Rows identify exposure status; columns identify infection status.
Each letter represents a count of people. For example, A is the number of exposed children who developed an infection.
A + B is the total exposed group; C + D is the total unexposed group.
These are the denominators for calculating risk in each group.



Before we calculate risk, relative risk, and absolute risk difference, we need to talk about 2x2 tables.

They are a really commonly used tool in epidemiology and biostatistics.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#exercise-risk-incidence-proportion
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#exercise-risk-incidence-proportion
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Exercise: Risk (Incidence Proportion)





Infection (+)
Infection (–)
Total

100
400
500


Not Exposed

Calculate Risk (Incidence Proportion)

Risk in the exposed = A / (A + B)
Risk in the unexposed = C / (C + D)


 


Take a moment to do this calculation on your own.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpretation-risk-incidence-proportion
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpretation-risk-incidence-proportion
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Interpretation: Risk (Incidence Proportion)

Risk in the exposed = 100 / 500 = 0.20 = 20%

20 out of every 100 exposed children developed an infection during follow-up.

Risk in the unexposed = 30 / 500 = 0.06 = 6%

6 out of every 100 unexposed children developed an infection during follow-up.




These findings are interesting, and we could stop here and report them.

But it can be handy to summarize them in a single measure, especially if we want to compare these results to other results.

We will discuss two options next.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#exercise-relative-risk-rr
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#exercise-relative-risk-rr
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies

Exercise: Relative Risk (RR)





Infection (+)
Infection (–)
Total

Take a moment to do this calculation on your own.

href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpretation-relative-risk-rr
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Interpretation: Relative Risk (RR)

RR = 0.20 ÷ 0.06 ≈ 3.33
Exposed children had about 3.33 times the risk of infection compared with unexposed children during follow-up.
Passive smoke exposure was associated with a substantial increase in risk during follow-up.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpretation-absolute-risk-difference-ard
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#interpretation-absolute-risk-difference-ard
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Interpretation: Absolute Risk Difference (ARD)

ARD = 0.20 − 0.06 = 0.14 = 14 percentage points
There were 14 more infections per 100 children in the exposed group than in the unexposed group during follow-up.
The risk difference describes the excess burden of disease associated with passive smoke exposure.



Helps answer the question, “If the association were causal, how many cases of disease could we eliminate?”

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#poll-interpreting-relative-risk
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#poll-interpreting-relative-risk
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Poll: Interpreting Relative Risk
In a cohort study examining smoking and cardiovascular disease, the Relative Risk (RR) for smokers compared to non-smokers is 1.50. What does this mean?
A. Smokers have a 50% lower risk of CVD
B. Smokers have a 50% higher risk of CVD
C. Smokers and non-smokers have the same risk
D. Smoking prevents cardiovascular disease


Correct Answer: B. Smokers have a 50% higher risk of CVD.
Brief Explanation: RR = 1.50 means smokers have 1.5 times the risk, which equals a 50% increase in risk compared to non-smokers.
What did we forget to say here?


Compared to non-smokers

Timeframe

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#poll-interpreting-risk-difference
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#poll-interpreting-risk-difference
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Poll: Interpreting Risk Difference
In a cohort study of smoking and cardiovascular disease (CVD), the risks over the same follow-up period are:

Risk in smokers = 20%; Risk in non-smokers = 10%
Absolute Risk Difference (ARD) = 20% − 10% = 10 percentage points

What does this ARD mean?
A. There were 10 more CVD cases per 100 smokers than per 100 non-smokers during follow-up
B. Smoking increases CVD risk by 10 times compared to non-smokers during follow-up
C. There was no association between smoking and CVD during follow-up
D. 10 out of every 100 cases of CVD were caused by smoking during follow-up


Correct Answer: A. There were 10 more CVD cases per 100 smokers than per 100 non-smokers during follow-up.
Brief Explanation: The observed CVD risk was 10 percentage points higher in smokers than in non-smokers over the same follow-up period (20% versus 10%).
This is an absolute difference in risk, not a relative increase of 10% or a tenfold increase. These results alone do not establish that smoking caused the difference.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#cohort-studies-strengths-and-limitations
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Experimental and Cohort Studies/Experimental and Cohort Studies.html#cohort-studies-strengths-and-limitations
title: Experimental and Cohort Studies
text:
Cohort Studies: Strengths and Limitations


Strengths

Directly measure incidence
Establish clear temporal sequence (Exposure → Outcome)
Study rare exposures efficiently
Examine multiple outcomes from one exposure


Limitations

Time-consuming and costly
Vulnerable to loss to follow-up
Potential exposure misclassification
Less efficient for rare diseases

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#hierarchy-of-study-designs
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#hierarchy-of-study-designs
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Hierarchy of Study Designs



Here is a review of our study design hierarchy.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-studies
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-studies
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Ecologic Studies

Ecologic studies compare groups, such as cities, schools, or countries.
Researchers analyze group characteristics, such as average income and average blood pressure.
They can describe population patterns and investigate questions about policies or environments.
A relationship between groups does not necessarily describe the relationship between individuals.



The important distinction is the level of the question and analysis.
Ecologic studies can address population questions directly, as well as generate hypotheses for individual-level research.
The hierarchy on the previous slide is a broad guide to individual causal inference, not a ranking of how well each design answers every possible question.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#unit-of-observation-vs.-unit-of-analysis
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#unit-of-observation-vs.-unit-of-analysis
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: Unit of Observation vs. Unit of Analysis
text:
Unit of Observation vs. Unit of Analysis
Hypothetical example: Measure residents’ income and blood pressure, then compare city averages.








Term
What Does It Mean?
In This Example




Unit of observation
The entity we collect measurements from
Each resident


Unit of analysis
The entity we compare and draw conclusions about
Each city



The same individual measurements could support a different analysis that compares residents instead of cities.


Definitions adapted from DeCarlo (2018).
Here the original observations are residents; aggregating their measurements changes the unit of analysis to cities.
If researchers receive only a table of city averages, their available observations are already at the city level.
Observation and analysis can be at the same level or different levels.
Do not teach that every ecologic study collects individual records.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-fallacy
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-fallacy
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Ecologic Fallacy
Ecologic fallacy: Assuming a relationship between groups also holds for individuals.

City averages alone do not reveal the relationships within cities.


These are invented teaching data, not evidence about income and blood pressure.
Each city contains five equally weighted observations. The left panel contains their exact means; the right panel shows the individual observations that produced them.
Income is the resident’s reported annual household income, and the blood-pressure measure is systolic blood pressure.
Ask students to describe each panel before explaining the error.
Between cities, higher average income accompanies higher average blood pressure. Within each city, higher-income residents have lower blood pressure in this constructed example. Neither pattern by itself establishes causation.
A reversal makes the distinction easy to see, but ecological fallacy does not require a reversal. The error is assuming an individual association from aggregate data alone, whether the unknown individual association is weaker, absent, reversed, or similar.

Concept: DeCarlo (2018). Figure generated from the hypothetical values in assets/ecologic-fallacy.R.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-what-can-we-conclude
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-what-can-we-conclude
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Practice: What Can We Conclude?
Suppose we have only the city averages from the previous slide. Which conclusion is supported?
A. Increasing a person’s income raises their blood pressure.
B. Within each city, richer residents have higher blood pressure.
C. Cities with higher average income have higher average blood pressure.
D. Income has no relationship with anyone’s blood pressure.

Answer: C. It stays at the level measured in the aggregate data. A adds a causal claim; B assumes an individual association; D also makes an unsupported individual claim. Ask students what information they would need to investigate B. Use a show of hands or letter cards if no live polling tool is configured.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#when-the-population-is-the-question
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#when-the-population-is-the-question
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: When the Population Is the Question
text:
When the Population Is the Question
Hypothetical question: After cities adopt a smoke-free indoor-air policy, do their heart-attack admission rates decline compared with cities that do not?

Exposure: A city policy that changes the shared environment.
Outcome: The city’s admission rate over time.
Why study groups? We want to evaluate the policy’s overall population effect, including effects on people who do not smoke.
The analysis must still consider other changes occurring in those cities.



So, why would we use an ecological study design?
This is a proposed study question, not a claim about a particular policy evaluation.
Comparing population trends before and after adoption, with suitable comparison cities, fits the policy question.
Individual smoking histories could add information, but they would not replace the question about changing a city’s policy.
A simple comparison of cities would not establish causality.
Ask what else might change at the same time, such as healthcare access or other tobacco policies.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#dietary-fat-and-breast-cancer-mortality
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#dietary-fat-and-breast-cancer-mortality
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: Dietary Fat and Breast Cancer Mortality
text:
Dietary Fat and Breast Cancer Mortality
The question: Could differences in diet help explain why breast cancer death rates differ across countries?
Sasaki et al. (1993)

Design: Ecologic study of 30 countries, using data from 1961 to 1986.
Exposure: National food-supply estimates per person, separated by fat type.
Outcome: Female breast cancer mortality rates.
Finding: Animal fat excluding fish fat was positively associated with mortality among women aged 50 and older. Fish fat showed inverse associations when statistically significant.


The country averages do not tell us what the women who died had eaten.



Start the story with a researcher looking across countries and wondering whether diet contributes to their different death rates.
Existing food-balance and mortality records allow a broad comparison without following individual diets for decades.
Distinguish national food supply from measured personal consumption.
This is an example of a research question, not a claim that this paper initiated the later trial.
What is the potential ecological fallacy we have to be careful to avoid?

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#low-fat-dietary-pattern-randomized-trial
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#low-fat-dietary-pattern-randomized-trial
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Low-Fat Dietary Pattern: Randomized Trial
A related question: Does assignment to a dietary program reduce new breast cancers?
Prentice et al. (2006)

Participants: 48,835 postmenopausal women, ages 50–79, without prior breast cancer.
Intervention: A program to reduce total fat and increase fruit, vegetables, and grains; comparison participants were not asked to change their diet.
Outcome: New invasive breast cancers during an average 8.1 years of follow-up.
2006 result: The intervention did not produce a statistically significant reduction in invasive breast cancer incidence.



Random assignment strengthens causal inference about assignment to this dietary program.
It does not isolate one fat type.
A nonsignificant result does not prove the effect is zero.
The trial’s reported hazard ratio was 0.91 (95% CI 0.83–1.01); interpreting hazard ratios is not required here. This slide summarizes the cited 2006 report, not subsequent follow-up publications.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-studies-strengths-and-limitations
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#ecologic-studies-strengths-and-limitations
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Ecologic Studies: Strengths and Limitations


Strengths

Fit questions about population policies and environments
Reveal patterns across places or time
Can use existing data efficiently


Limitations

Group associations may not describe individuals
Averages can hide differences within groups
Other population differences can complicate interpretation


Choose the design that fits the question and the level of the conclusion.


Return to the policy example: an ecologic design can be appropriate because the question concerns a population intervention, even when individual data are available.
In the dietary study, national food supply is an imperfect proxy for consumption.
Ecologic analyses can account for measured population characteristics, but aggregate data do not automatically resolve confounding or differences in measurement between places.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#group-discussion-comparing-study-designs
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#group-discussion-comparing-study-designs
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Group Discussion: Comparing Study Designs
Work in groups of 2–3 for 4 minutes. Prepare a brief explanation for each question.









Ecologic Study
Randomized Trial




Unit of analysis
Countries
Individual women


Exposure / intervention
National supply of different fats
Assignment to a dietary program


Outcome
Breast cancer mortality
Invasive breast cancer incidence




Why does the ecologic study not tell us whether changing one woman’s diet would change her risk?
What does random assignment add, and what dietary question does this trial actually test?
Why would it be misleading to say that this trial simply proves or disproves the ecologic study?


 

Purpose: practice matching conclusions to the question, unit of analysis, and design. This is not a competition to name the universally best design.
Facilitation: allow four minutes, then invite a different group to answer each question. Keep the table visible.
Answer key:

The country records do not link each woman’s own exposure to her outcome. Other national differences could contribute to the pattern. Access to effective treatment is one possible influence on mortality; it is a discussion hypothesis, not a finding established by this paper. Mortality involves both developing cancer and surviving it.
Random assignment helps make the groups comparable at baseline. The trial tests assignment to a program with several dietary goals; adherence still matters.
Exposure definitions, populations, and outcomes differ. A stronger design for one causal question does not turn it into a test of every related question. Ask students to name at least two differences from the table.

Sources: Sasaki et al. (1993); Prentice et al. (2006).

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#from-study-design-to-trustworthy-comparisons
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#from-study-design-to-trustworthy-comparisons
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: From Study Design to Trustworthy Comparisons
text:
From Study Design to Trustworthy Comparisons
The two dietary studies asked different questions. For either study, we still need to ask what could make the comparison misleading.

Selection: Who entered the study, and who stayed in it?
Information: Were exposure and outcome measured accurately?
Confounding: Did the groups differ in other causes of the outcome?

We will connect these questions to the bias examples from the case-control lecture.

This is the transition from choosing a study design to evaluating the comparison it produces.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#social-desirability-bias
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#social-desirability-bias
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Social Desirability Bias

Definition: Participants report what seems socially acceptable instead of what actually happened.
Example: Someone understates their alcohol use because they worry the interviewer will judge them.
Problem: The recorded answer differs from the behavior we want to measure.
Reducing it: Use neutral questions and protect participants’ privacy.



Neutral wording can help, but it does not guarantee accurate reporting.
Explain why responses are confidential and consider private self-administered questions when appropriate.
Contrast reporting less drinking with actually drinking less because of being observed.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#hawthorne-effect
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#hawthorne-effect
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Hawthorne Effect

Definition: People change their behavior because they know they are being observed.
Example: Participants walk more while a research team monitors their activity.
Their recorded activity may be accurate, but it may differ from their usual activity.

Changing behavior and reporting behavior inaccurately are different problems.


Observation-related behavior change is not automatically measurement error.
Its implications depend on the question: are we interested in usual activity outside a study or activity during a monitored intervention? Preserve this distinction in the exercise.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-bias-and-behavior-changes
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-bias-and-behavior-changes
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Practice: Bias and Behavior Changes
For each scenario, identify the bias or behavior change and explain why.

Parents of sick children recall pesticide exposure during pregnancy more carefully than parents of healthy children.
Participants underreport alcohol use because they worry that the interviewer will judge them.
Outcome assessors know who received treatment and rate those participants more favorably.
Interviewers ask lung cancer cases more detailed exposure questions than they ask controls.
Participants exercise more because they know their activity is being monitored.


Ask for a brief explanation before revealing the next scenario. These mechanisms are stipulated for the exercise; they are not inferred from observed differences alone.

Recall bias: exposure recall differs between groups.
Social desirability bias: concern about judgment changes the report.
Observer bias: treatment knowledge influences outcome ratings.
Interviewer bias: exposure questioning differs between groups.
Hawthorne effect: observation changes actual behavior. An accurate measurement of that changed behavior is not itself an information error.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#review-sample-size-and-bias
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#review-sample-size-and-bias
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Review: Sample Size and Bias

Random error (sampling variability): Results vary by chance. More observations generally improve precision.
Bias: A systematic problem in selection or measurement can remain even in a very large study.

Example: Interviewing more people at local gyms does not fix the problem of estimating community activity from a sample that overrepresents gym users.
For bias, improve who is included or how measurements are made. Increasing the sample size alone does not repair those processes.


This example concerns estimating community activity, not every possible comparison among gym users.
A large biased sample can give a very precise answer to the wrong population question.
Then transition: even with careful recruitment and accurate measurement, groups can differ in other causes of the outcome.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#review-confounding
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#review-confounding
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Review: Confounding
Confounding: Other causes of the outcome get mixed into our estimate of the exposure’s effect. We may give credit or blame to the wrong variable.









Would reducing ice cream sales reduce drownings? This pattern alone does not show that it would.


The arrows express the simplified causal assumptions, not estimates from data.
Warm weather can raise sales and increase opportunities for swimming. The observed association may be useful for prediction without being the causal effect of ice cream sales.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-does-the-class-increase-falls
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-does-the-class-increase-falls
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: Practice: Does the Class Increase Falls?
text:
Practice: Does the Class Increase Falls?
Hypothetical study: Follow 200 people for one year after some choose to attend a fall-prevention class.




People With at Least One Fall
People Followed
One-Year Risk




Attended class
28
100
28%


Did not attend
12
100
12%



Which conclusion is justified?
A. The class caused more falls.
B. Attendees had more falls, but they may have differed before class.
C. The class prevented falls.

Answer: B. These are invented counts for teaching, not findings about an actual program. Assume complete follow-up and accurate measurement so we can focus on confounding. The outcome is whether each person had at least one fall during the same one-year period, not the total number of falls.
Ask what might lead someone to join: a prior fall may both encourage attendance and predict future falls. Participants chose whether to attend; they were not randomized.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#comparing-people-with-the-same-fall-history
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#comparing-people-with-the-same-fall-history
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
section: Comparing People With the Same Fall History
text:
Comparing People With the Same Fall History
The same 200 people, now separated by whether they had fallen before the class began:










No Prior Fall
Prior Fall
All Participants




Attended class
1 / 10 = 10%
27 / 90 = 30%
28 / 100 = 28%


Did not attend
9 / 90 = 10%
3 / 10 = 30%
12 / 100 = 12%




Within each history group, the risks are the same.
Attendees included more people with prior falls: 90% versus 10%.

Accounting for fall history removes the apparent difference in this example.


Start with the rightmost column, “All Participants.” These are the same totals we just saw: 28 of 100 class attendees and 12 of 100 nonattendees had at least one fall during follow-up.
The rows still separate people by whether they attended the class, just as in the previous table. The “No Prior Fall” and “Prior Fall” columns now divide each attendance group by whether people had fallen before the class began.
In each cell, the first number is the number of people who had at least one fall during the following year. The second number is the total number of people in that particular attendance and fall-history group.
For example, read the first cell under “No Prior Fall” as: “Of the 10 class attendees with no prior fall, 1 fell during follow-up, a risk of 10%.” Then move down that column: among nonattendees with no prior fall, 9 of 90 fell, also 10%.
Now read down the “Prior Fall” column: 27 of 90 attendees and 3 of 10 nonattendees fell during follow-up. Both risks are 30%. Reading down each fall-history column lets us compare attendance groups with the same prior fall history.
This is stratification: compare people within categories of a relevant variable.
Students should interpret the supplied percentages; calculation or a pooled adjustment formula is not required.
All people and falls remain in the table. We changed the comparison, not the observations.
In this hypothetical story, previous falls influence attendance and predict subsequent falls.
Those risks became mixed into the overall comparison. If both groups had an equal mix of the two history categories, each would have a 20% risk: the average of 10% and 30%. This optional illustration is standardization, not an additional result students must calculate.
Equal observed risks do not prove that a real intervention has no effect, nor does any change after adjustment prove confounding. Here the constructed numbers and stated causal assumptions illustrate the mechanism. Sources for stratification and interpretation: Dicker (2025).

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#prior-falls-and-class-attendance
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#prior-falls-and-class-attendance
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Prior Falls and Class Attendance
In our hypothetical study, prior falls can influence both class attendance and the chance of falling again.









In this hypothetical example, assume the class has no effect on falls.
The groups’ different fall histories explain the overall difference in risk.


Read each arrow in ordinary language. In this hypothetical story, having fallen before can motivate someone to attend the class and can increase their chance of falling again. Each arrow represents a proposed causal influence.
There is no arrow from class attendance to falls in the next year because we assume the class has no causal effect in this hypothetical example. This is an assumption of the teaching story, not a conclusion established by the table alone.
Connect the diagram to the tables: 90% of attendees had a prior fall, compared with 10% of nonattendees. Their different fall histories produced the overall risk difference, which we could mistakenly attribute to class attendance.
Comparing attendees and nonattendees within the same fall-history category gave equal risks in our constructed example. The diagram explains why we considered fall history. The numbers alone do not establish the arrows or prove that a real class has no effect.
Ask students to explain why prior falls matter for both attendance and future falls. Formal diagram terminology and path rules are not needed here. General diagram principles: Hernán et al. (2002).

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-which-variable-needs-attention
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#practice-which-variable-needs-attention
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Practice: Which Variable Needs Attention?
A study compares people who choose a fall-prevention class with people who do not.
Researchers learn that prior falls influence class attendance and the chance of another fall.
What is the best reason to consider prior falls when making the comparison?
A. We should control for every variable available.
B. Prior falls are a plausible common cause of attendance and later falls.
C. Any variable associated with the outcome must be controlled.

Answer: B. The stated causal knowledge identifies the reason for concern. Associations alone do not establish a variable’s role. A and C overlook mediators, colliders, and the question being asked. Use a show of hands or letter cards as a low-tech fallback.
This replaces the abstract inherited true/false questions with a question about the worked example. Students should explain the common cause, not select a statistical model.

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#addressing-confounding-during-study-design
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#addressing-confounding-during-study-design
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Addressing Confounding During Study Design








Approach
Basic Idea
Example




Randomization
Assign the intervention by chance
Randomly offer the class


Restriction
Limit a relevant characteristic
Enroll only people with no prior falls


Matching
Select comparison participants with similar characteristics
Match participants on fall history



Randomization balances baseline factors on average, including factors we did not measure.
Restriction narrows the population studied. Matching still requires an appropriate analysis.

This is a conceptual menu, not instruction in conducting a matched analysis. Random assignment does not guarantee identical groups in a particular sample, and it does not solve every problem arising after assignment. Restriction or matching only addresses the relevant factors selected and measured; neither automatically removes all confounding. Matching on the wrong variables can also introduce problems. Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2024); Dicker (2025).

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#addressing-confounding-during-analysis
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#addressing-confounding-during-analysis
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
Addressing Confounding During Analysis

Stratification: Compare exposed and unexposed people within categories of a confounder, as in the fall-history table.
Statistical adjustment: Use methods such as regression or standardization to account for appropriate measured factors.
Both approaches depend on choosing relevant variables and measuring them adequately.

When reading a study, ask: What did the researchers account for, why did they choose those factors, and what important differences might remain?

Students need to recognize these approaches and explain their purpose; they do not need to fit a regression model or calculate an adjusted effect. Confounding can remain when important factors are missing or measured poorly. Methods also rely on design and modeling assumptions. These methods do not make an observational comparison equivalent to randomization merely because an estimate is labeled “adjusted.” Source: Dicker (2025).

objectID: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#from-concepts-to-your-presentation
href: Module 06-07 - Analytic Epidemiology/Ecologic Studies and Confounding/Ecologic Studies and Confounding.html#from-concepts-to-your-presentation
title: Ecologic Studies and Confounding
text:
From Concepts to Your Presentation


The Conceptual Progression

Descriptive epidemiology: Describe patterns and generate hypotheses.
Analytic epidemiology: Evaluate exposure–outcome relationships.
Critical thinking: Distinguish association from causation.


For Group Presentation 1

Describe population patterns using appropriate epidemiologic measures.
Include and cite at least one source of analytic evidence.
Explain the evidence type, exposure, outcome, and main finding.
Relate the evidence to your findings; discuss limitations, bias, and confounding.
Avoid definitive causal claims or policy recommendations.


Use the assignment instructions and rubric in D2L for the full requirements.

Source: Group Presentation 1 assignment instructions, sections 3–6, in the course’s Assignments/Group Presentation 1 folder.
Acceptable analytic evidence includes peer-reviewed studies, government or public health reports, surveillance reports with analytic comparisons, and textbooks or course readings that synthesize analytic findings. A single primary research study is not required. Students should explain how their selected evidence supports or contextualizes their descriptive patterns without claiming it proves a causal explanation.
This slide highlights the connection to our epidemiology lessons. The assignment also specifies presentation structure, timing, participation, slide design, and submission expectations; students should consult the full assignment and rubric in D2L.

In epidemiology, we often want to describe the “typical” person in a population or subpopulation.

When we analyze data to do so, we call it “descriptive analysis”.

When conducting descriptive analysis, the method we choose will depend on the type of data we’re analyzing.

At the most basic level, variables can be described as numerical (quantitative) or categorical (qualitative).

We reviewed this distinction last time.

Our focus today will be on numerical variables.

Numerical variables can then be further divided into continuous and discrete.

Question: What is the difference between continuous and discrete numerical variables?
- The distinction is whether the variable can take on a continuum of values or only a certain set of values.
Question: Can you think of some examples?
- Continuous examples: Height, weight, and sleep duration.
- Discrete examples: Number of drinks, number of household members, number of clinic visits.

For all types and subtypes of variables, there are both numerical and graphical methods we can use for descriptive analysis.

We’ll also discuss some additional graphical summaries of our data today.

Graphical summaries are just visual representations of our data.

Often, they lack the detail and precision of numerical summaries, but they are generally better for quickly getting a “feel” for the center, spread, and shape of our data.

Additionally, graphical summaries tend to be better for making quick, general comparisons. For example, comparing two groups.

We will then bring the numerical and graphical summaries together in Excel and practice writing interpretations supported by the data.

Before moving on, let’s quickly review the characteristics of the mean, median, and mode.

Why Not Always Use the Median? Because the mean…
- Uses All Data Information: The mean incorporates every single number in the dataset. The median only looks at the middle rank, meaning it completely ignores how large or small the outer values are.
- Mathematical and Algebraic Convenience: The mean behaves well in equations, calculus, and further statistical tests (such as variance, standard deviation, and regression analysis). The median is harder to work with mathematically because it relies on ordering rather than a linear formula.
- Higher Statistical Efficiency: For symmetric or normal distributions, the mean has lower variability from sample to sample (higher statistical efficiency). The median requires a larger sample size to achieve the same level of precision.
- When Extremes Matter: If you are measuring total resource needs (like total weight, total income for tax revenue, or total water consumption), you want those large outliers. Using a median would hide the true sum of the data.

text:
Variance



The variance is a measure of dispersion that is slightly more complicated to calculate, but it gives us a number we can use to quantify the dispersion of heights around the mean.

To do this, let’s work through a simple example that only includes six observations: 3 people who are 58 inches tall and 3 people who are 78 inches tall.

In this sample of six people from our population, the average height is 68 inches.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#variance-1
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#variance-1
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Variance


Next, let’s draw an imaginary line straight up from the mean.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#distances-from-the-mean
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#distances-from-the-mean
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Distances from the Mean



Then, let’s measure the difference, or distance, between each person’s height and the mean height.

Read each deviation as observation minus mean: 58 - 68 = -10; 78 - 68 = +10.

Three deviations are -10 and three are +10. Their sum is zero despite visible variation.

Question 1. Remember, our goal is to measure how much distance there is, on average, between the mean height and individual heights. If we stop here, we get zero. Does that mean there is no variation in heights?
- No, there is clearly variation in the heights.

Why do we get zero?



Because the positive and negative differences cancel each other out.


Can you think of a way we could avoid cancellation?



Don’t give the answer. Move to the next slide.

Square the Differences



Let’s square the differences.

href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#from-squared-distances-to-variance
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
From Squared Distances to Variance



Then we add up all the squared differences.

Is 600 square inches the sample variance?

No!

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#variance-2
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#variance-2
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Variance

s2=6006−1=120s^2 = \dfrac{600}{6-1} = 120 square inches.


We divide by n, the number of non-missing observations, minus 1. In this case n equals six, so n-1 equals five.

The result is 120 square inches.

The n-minus-one adjustment is used for sample variance.

text:
Exercise: Comparing Distributions


Open practice_data.xlsx.

Select the comparing_distributions sheet.

Complete the Comparisons table.



For all the columns, the mean is 68 inches.

For the column “all_68” the variance and standard deviation are both zero.

When comparing the rest of the columns notice that all of them have a non-zero variance. This is because not all people have the same value in that column – they vary.

Additionally, we can see very clearly that variance (and standard deviation) are affected by at least two things:

The second property of the data that is clearly influencing variance is the width of the range of values included in the distribution. For example, even_48_88 has a larger variance and standard deviation than even_58_78, even though both are evenly distributed across the range of possible values. The reason is because the range of possible values is larger, and therefore the range of distances from the mean is larger too.

First is the distribution of values across the range of possible values. For example, half_58_78 and half_48_88 have a larger variance than even_58_78 and even_48_88 because all the values are clustered at the min and max - far away from the mean.

Z-Scores: Distance in SD Units

z=value−meanstandard deviationz = \frac{\text{value} - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}





Z-score
Interpretation




Positive
Above the mean


0

Standard deviation describes the spread of a distribution. A z-score uses that spread to describe where one value is located relative to the mean.

The magnitude tells us how many SDs the value is from the mean.

section: Check: Calculate and Interpret a Z-Score
text:
Check: Calculate and Interpret a Z-Score
A fictional score distribution has mean 30 and SD 5.
What is the z-score for a value of 20?

z=20−305=−2z = \frac{20-30}{5} = -2
The value is 2 standard deviations below the mean.



Ask why the answer is negative; a negative z-score is not a negative raw score.

Follow up verbally: a value of 35 has z = 1; a value of 30 has z = 0.

But why would we want to do this?

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#z-scores-why
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#z-scores-why
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Z-Scores: Why?











Health assessment
Maria’s score
Reference mean
SD
Z-score




Physical functioning
85
75
5
+2


Emotional well-being
90
80
10
+1






Both health assessments are scored from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better health.
Maria’s emotional well-being score is higher in absolute terms: 90 compared with 85 for physical functioning.
For physical functioning, z = (85 - 75) / 5 = +2.
For emotional well-being, z = (90 - 80) / 10 = +1.
Maria’s physical functioning score is therefore stronger relative to its reference population, even though its raw score is lower.
The z-scores describe relative standing. They do not tell us which health domain is more important or whether either score is clinically meaningful.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#quartiles-and-the-middle-half
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#quartiles-and-the-middle-half
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Quartiles and the Middle Half









Position
Meaning
Sleep hours




Q1
25th percentile
6.00 hours


Q2
50th percentile (Median)
6.750 hours


Q3
75th percentile
7.625 hours


IQR
Q3 − Q1
1.625 hours






The final numerical summary we’ll discuss today is quartiles.

Quartiles mark positions in the ordered observations.

Q1 is the value at or below which approximately 25% of the observations fall.

Q2 is the value at or below which approximately 50% of the observations fall. It is also the median.

Q3 is the value at or below which approximately 75% of the observations fall.

The IQR describes the width of the middle half of a distribution.

With small samples, interpolation conventions can produce slightly different quartiles; these use Excel QUARTILE.INC’s convention.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#calculate-quartiles-in-excel
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#calculate-quartiles-in-excel
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Calculate Quartiles in Excel









Position
Excel formula
Result




Q1
=QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,1)



Q2
=QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,2)



Q3
=QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,3)



IQR
=G13-G11 or



IQR
=QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,3) - QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,1)







Now, let’s calculate quartiles using Excel.

Demonstration:
- Open the height_and_weight sheet in Excel.
- Type Q1: in cell F11.
- Type =QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,1) in cell G11.
- Type Q2: in cell F12.
- Type =QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,2) in cell G12.
- Type Q3: in cell F13.
- Type =QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,3) in cell G13.
- Type IQR: in cell F14.
- Type =G13-G11 or =QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,3) - QUARTILE.INC(C2:C21,1) in cell G12.
Additional information
- With small samples, interpolation conventions can produce slightly different quartiles; these use Excel QUARTILE.INC’s convention.
- A quartile does not have to equal an observed value.
