href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#choosing-a-chartgraph-for-one-variable
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
section: Choosing a Chart/Graph for One Variable
text:
Choosing a Chart/Graph for One Variable




Variable Type
Usually Appropriate




Categorical
Bar chartPie chart


Continuous Numerical
HistogramBoxplotDensity plot


Discrete Numerical
Bar chartHistogramDot plot






In the same way that the variable type will determine the numerical summaries we can use, it will also determine the graphical summaries we can use.

This table doesn’t represent the entire universe of chart/graph types. It presents only some common ones that we will discuss.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#histograms
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#histograms
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Histograms












A histogram groups numerical values into intervals called bins.

The horizontal axis shows the values and their units.
The height of each bar shows how many observations fall in that bin.
The bars touch because the bins cover adjacent intervals.

Use the pattern of bars to examine the distribution’s shape and spread.



Contrast a histogram with a bar chart: histogram bins represent ordered numerical intervals, not separate categories.
Ask students what the tallest bar means in the context of sleep duration.
Counts across all bins should add up to the sample size, 12 students here.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#reading-distribution-shape-in-a-histogram
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#reading-distribution-shape-in-a-histogram
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
section: Reading Distribution Shape in a Histogram
text:
Reading Distribution Shape in a Histogram

Name skew by the direction of the longer tail.


Ask students to point to the tail of each skewed distribution.
Symmetric does not necessarily mean normal; a distribution can also have multiple peaks.
Do not promise a stable distribution shape from a very small sample.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#a-bimodal-distribution-has-two-peaks
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#a-bimodal-distribution-has-two-peaks
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
section: A Bimodal Distribution Has Two Peaks
text:
A Bimodal Distribution Has Two Peaks

Bimodal means that the distribution has two distinct peaks.


The data are fictional and were constructed to make the two peaks easy to see.
Ask students to identify each peak before introducing the term bimodal.
Two peaks can suggest that the data combine subgroups, but the histogram alone cannot identify the subgroups or explain the pattern.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#check-which-direction-is-the-skew
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#check-which-direction-is-the-skew
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
section: Check: Which Direction Is the Skew?
text:
Check: Which Direction Is the Skew?

Most clinic visits last 15-25 minutes, but a few last 60-90 minutes.
A. Left-skewed
B. Right-skewed
C. The long visits make the distribution symmetric

B. Right-skewed. The long visits extend the tail toward larger values.



Give students 30 seconds to choose, then have them explain to a neighbor before voting.
Use raised fingers or written letters; no polling service is required.
The scenario is fictional and concerns visit duration, not a clinical recommendation.
Distinguish where most observations lie from the direction the tail extends.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#histogram-bin-width-changes-the-picture
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#histogram-bin-width-changes-the-picture
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
section: Histogram: Bin Width Changes the Picture
text:
Histogram: Bin Width Changes the Picture

Did the students’ sleep change, or only how we grouped it?

Only the grouping changed. Inspect more than one sensible bin width.



Both panels contain exactly the same twelve values and use common axis scales.
Wide bins hide detail; very narrow bins can make a small sample appear irregular.
Look for clusters, gaps, and possible outliers without declaring every irregularity meaningful.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#create-a-histogram-in-excel
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#create-a-histogram-in-excel
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Create a Histogram in Excel

Select B1:B13, including the sleep_hours header.
Choose Insert → Statistic Chart → Histogram.
Add a clear title and axis titles: Sleep duration (hours) and Number of students.
Inspect the bins. Try a 1-hour bin width and compare with the automatic grouping.

Do the plotted counts add up to 12?


On some versions, use Insert → Recommended Charts → All Charts → Histogram.
Use Chart Design → Add Chart Element for axis titles where available.
Windows bin controls are generally under Format Axis → Axis Options. Mac controls may appear under Format Data Series; interface wording depends on the version.
Read the displayed interval labels. Excel’s treatment of boundary values may differ from the left-closed bins in the teaching graph, even with the same bin width.
Avoid a Pareto chart, which orders bars by frequency rather than numerical position.
Microsoft histogram instructions: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/create-a-histogram

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#describe-what-you-can-see
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#describe-what-you-can-see
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Describe What You Can See
A useful histogram description addresses:

Shape: where values cluster and which direction any tail extends.
Spread: the observed values and units.
Possible outliers: observations that stand apart and warrant checking.



Demonstrate by describing the displayed Excel histogram, using its actual bin boundaries.
For the sleep sample, values span 5-9 hours and most observations fall between 6 and 8 hours; avoid insisting it has a precise population distribution shape.
A histogram supports descriptive statements; it does not establish causal effects or representativeness.
Connect this wording directly to Prep 3’s requested histogram observations.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#boxplots
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#boxplots
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Boxplots












A boxplot gives a compact summary of a numerical distribution.

It shows the distribution’s center and spread.
Its compact form makes groups easy to compare on the same scale.
It can flag observations that fall far from the middle of the data.

A boxplot can hide peaks, gaps, and sample size. Inspect the raw data or a histogram too.



Each dot represents one fictional student’s sleep duration. The boxplot summarizes those same twelve values.
Read values along the vertical axis. The horizontal position only separates overlapping dots.
Use the next slide to identify the median, quartiles, IQR, and whiskers.
A boxplot does not require the distribution to be symmetric or normal.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#reading-a-boxplot
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#reading-a-boxplot
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Reading a Boxplot


Line inside the box: median.
Lower and upper box edges: Q1 and Q3. Box height: IQR.
Whiskers and separate points show values beyond the middle half.



Ask students to locate the three quartiles from the previous slide.
The height of the box shows the IQR because the numerical values run vertically.
A boxplot summarizes the distribution but can hide multiple peaks; inspect the histogram too.
Adapted from Yan slide 43.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#whiskers-and-potential-outliers
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#whiskers-and-potential-outliers
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Whiskers and Potential Outliers
For the boxplots in this lesson:

Fences are Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
Whiskers reach the most extreme observed values within the fences.
Values beyond the fences appear as separate points.



Whiskers do not necessarily reach the minimum and maximum of the whole dataset.
The fences are calculated cutoffs; the whisker endpoints are actual observations.
A flagged point may be a valid observation. It is not automatically an error or proof of a different population.
Other boxplot conventions exist; this is the convention used in the displayed plots.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#check-compare-these-boxplots
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#check-compare-these-boxplots
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Check: Compare These Boxplots

Which group has the higher median? Larger IQR? A flagged outlier?

B: higher median and larger IQR. A: a flagged point at 35.



Give students one minute to answer all three questions before revealing the response.
Group A is the workbook’s stress_score variable; group B is an additional fictional comparison.
Group A median = 17.5 and IQR = 5.5; group B median = 23 and IQR = 11.
Group A’s upper fence is 28.75, so 35 is flagged; the upper whisker ends at 25.
Adapted from Yan slide 44. This checks the boxplot skill required by Quiz 4 with a different example.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#creating-a-boxplot-in-excel
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#creating-a-boxplot-in-excel
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Creating a Boxplot in Excel

Select B1:B13, including the sleep_hours header.
Choose Insert → Statistic Chart → Box & Whisker.
Change the chart title to Sleep Duration and add the vertical axis title Hours.
Right-click the box and choose Format Data Series. Select Show inner points to display each student’s value.

Find the median and IQR. Does Excel flag any potential outliers?

Median = 6.75 hours; IQR = 1.625 hours. Excel flags no potential outliers.



On some versions, use Insert → Recommended Charts → All Charts → Box & Whisker.
Ask students to create the chart before revealing the answer.
The lower and upper edges of the box are Q1 = 6 and Q3 = 7.625 hours, so IQR = 7.625 − 6 = 1.625 hours.
Excel’s default quartile setting may differ by version. If needed, open Format Data Series and choose Inclusive Median to match QUARTILE.INC and the values used in this lesson.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#bar-chart
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#bar-chart
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Bar Chart

Open the height_and_weight sheet and select A1:B21, including the headers.
Choose Insert → PivotTable. Place the PivotTable in a new worksheet.
Drag sex to Rows and id to Values. Confirm that Values displays Count of id.
Select the PivotTable and choose Insert → Bar Chart → 2-D Clustered Bar.
Title the chart Students by Sex. Label the horizontal axis Number of students.



Ask students to create the PivotTable and chart before revealing the answer.
If Excel summarizes id as Sum of id, open Value Field Settings and select Count.
The PivotTable should show Female = 12, Male = 6, and (blank) = 2.
Keep the blank category visible. Removing it would hide two records with missing sex values.
A bar chart uses separate bars for categories. The bars do not touch because the categories are distinct rather than adjacent numerical intervals.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#density-plot
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#density-plot
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Density Plot












A density plot shows a smoothed estimate of a distribution’s shape.

Higher parts of the curve indicate where observations are more concentrated.
The total area under the curve equals 1.
The amount of smoothing affects the curve.

With only 12 observations, use this plot as a rough summary.



This graph uses the same twelve fictional sleep values as the histogram and boxplot.
A density plot does not show counts. Its vertical scale represents density, and the total area under the curve equals 1.
The curve extends slightly beyond the observed minimum and maximum because the smoothing method places a small amount of density around each observation.
With such a small sample, avoid treating bumps in the curve as stable features of a larger population.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#dot-plot
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#dot-plot
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Dot Plot












A dot plot displays the individual observations.

Each dot represents one student.
Dots stack when students report the same value.
Gaps and repeated values remain visible.

Dot plots work especially well for small datasets.



Ask students to confirm that the graph contains twelve dots.
The tallest stacks occur at 6, 6.5, 7, and 8 hours, with two students at each value.
Unlike a density plot, this graph preserves every observed value and directly shows the small sample size.
The vertical position only separates repeated observations; it does not represent a separate measured variable.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#group-exercise-describe-stress-scores
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#group-exercise-describe-stress-scores

text:
Group Exercise: Describe Stress Scores
Use stress_score in C2:C13 from the same practice file.

Calculate n, mean, sample SD, minimum, and maximum.
Create a histogram with a title and labeled axes.
Write three observations about shape, spread, and possible outliers.
Be ready to explain one number and one feature of your graph.

Work for 8 minutes. We will use 4 minutes to compare answers.


Minutes 65-77: eight minutes of work plus four minutes of debrief.
Work in groups of three or four; assign an Excel operator, a range/formula checker, and an interpreter.
Change B2:B13 to C2:C13; do not include the output summary cells in the input range.
If Excel access fails, use the following data and displayed graph to write interpretations; use a calculator for the mean and range.
These fictional practice scores do not establish any health threshold.

href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#practice-data-and-graph
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Practice Data and Graph


Stress scores, sorted:
12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22, 25, 35
Describe the distribution in your own words.













Leave this slide visible during group work; keep the debrief answers on the next slide.
Use an ordinary classroom timer for the eight minutes; no additional interactive infrastructure is needed.
These bins include their lower boundary and exclude their upper boundary; Excel bins can group boundary observations differently.
Students can describe the broad pattern even when bin boundaries differ.

objectID: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#group-exercise-compare-your-results
href: Module 08 - Statistics Overview and Descriptive Statistics/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs/Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs.html#group-exercise-compare-your-results
title: Continuous Data Summaries and Graphs
text:
Group Exercise: Compare Your Results



Summary
stress_score




n
12


Mean
19.00 points


Sample SD
6.19 points

12; 35 points




Most scores lie between 12 and 25, with a tail toward higher scores.
Observed scores span 23 points.
35 stands apart and warrants checking; it is not automatically an error.



Ask groups for their values before advancing to this slide.
Ask one group to explain its SD in terms of variability among the twelve scores, not uncertainty in the mean.
Accept descriptions that match their histogram rather than requiring identical phrasing.
The 35-point observation is also the flagged point in the earlier group A boxplot.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#a-scale-that-always-reads-high
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#a-scale-that-always-reads-high
title: Reliability and Validity
section: A Scale That Always Reads High
text:
A Scale That Always Reads High
A wellness team checks a scale with a known 60 kg calibration mass.



Reading 1
Reading 2
Reading 3




65 kg
65 kg
65 kg



The readings agree with one another. Each is 5 kg above the reference.
Would repeating this measurement many more times solve the problem?

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#consistency-and-accuracy
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#consistency-and-accuracy
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Consistency and Accuracy
Reliability concerns consistency under comparable conditions when what we measure has not changed.
Measurement validity concerns whether a measure supports the intended interpretation: does it measure what we want it to measure?
The scale is repeatable but inaccurate. Repeating it does not remove the 5 kg bias. It needs calibration or correction before use.
Reliable measurements can still be wrong.


For a physical calibration mass, accuracy is easy to assess against a reference. For constructs such as stress, validity requires several kinds of evidence.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#why-measurements-differ
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#why-measurements-differ
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Why Measurements Differ



Explanation
Example
What to Check




True change
The mass on the scale actually changes
Whether the object changed


Systematic error
The scale reads 5 kg high each time
Calibration against a reference


Random error
Readings fluctuate under otherwise identical conditions
Repeatability and procedures



A change in a score does not, by itself, show that a program worked.


Random error reduces consistency. Systematic error can preserve consistency while undermining accuracy.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#reliability-over-time
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#reliability-over-time
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Reliability Over Time
Test–retest reliability: the same people take the same instrument on separate occasions, during a period when the underlying characteristic should be stable.
Intra-rater reliability: the same rater scores the same material again. For example, one instructor scores the same recorded presentation twice.
The key distinction is whether we are studying the instrument across occasions or the repeatability of one person’s judgments.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#reliability-across-raters-and-forms
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#reliability-across-raters-and-forms
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Reliability Across Raters and Forms
Inter-rater reliability: different raters independently score the same material using the same criteria.
Example: two instructors score the same recorded presentation.
Parallel-forms reliability: people complete two versions designed to measure the same construct with equivalent content and difficulty.
Example: two equivalent forms of a vocabulary test. Merely using two different tests does not make them equivalent.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#internal-consistency
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#internal-consistency
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Internal Consistency
Internal consistency asks whether items intended to measure the same construct are related to one another.
A stress scale might ask about feeling overwhelmed and difficulty relaxing. These items should have a meaningful relationship if they reflect the same construct.
Internal consistency alone does not establish that the scale measures stress accurately or covers all important aspects of stress.


No calculation of alpha or other internal-consistency coefficients is required for this lesson.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-types-of-reliability
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-types-of-reliability
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Question: Types of Reliability
Match each situation to a reliability type.

Two observers independently score the same video.
One observer scores that video again a week later.
Students repeat the same stable-attribute questionnaire after a week.
Students complete equivalent versions A and B of a test.
Researchers examine relationships among items on a stress scale.

Choices: inter-rater, intra-rater, test–retest, parallel-forms, internal consistency.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answers-types-of-reliability
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answers-types-of-reliability
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Answers: Types of Reliability



Situation
Reliability Type




Two observers
Inter-rater


One observer scoring again
Intra-rater


Same questionnaire over time
Test–retest


Equivalent test versions
Parallel-forms


Related items within a scale
Internal consistency



For repeated measurements, consider actual change, memory, and practice effects before interpreting differences as measurement error.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#improving-measurement-consistency
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#improving-measurement-consistency
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Improving Measurement Consistency

Use clear instructions and the same measurement conditions.
Train raters with a shared scoring rubric and practice examples.
Check equipment against known references.
Review ambiguous items and scoring rules.

A reliability coefficient summarizes a particular kind of consistency. Its interpretation depends on the method, population, and intended use. There is no single cutoff that makes every measure acceptable.


Retain the introductory idea that higher reliability usually means more consistency, without teaching a universal 0.70 acceptance rule.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-a-consistent-error
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-a-consistent-error
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Question: A Consistent Error
A scale gives almost identical readings each time, but all readings are 5 kg too high. Which statement is best supported?
A. It is reliable and accurate for measuring mass.
B. It is repeatable, but the readings have a systematic error.
C. It is accurate because repeated readings agree.
D. More repetitions will necessarily remove the error.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answer-a-consistent-error
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answer-a-consistent-error
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Answer: A Consistent Error
B. The readings are repeatable but systematically too high.
Reliability is necessary, but not sufficient, for valid measurement. A measure that changes unpredictably cannot support dependable interpretations.
Consistency alone does not show that the measure captures the intended quantity or construct. One correct reading by chance does not establish validity either.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#three-questions-about-validity
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#three-questions-about-validity
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Three Questions About Validity



Concept
Main Question




Measurement validity
Does the measure capture the intended quantity or construct?


Internal validity
Is the study’s conclusion credible, given bias and confounding?


External validity
Do the findings apply to other people, settings, or times?



For a causal claim, internal validity includes whether alternative explanations have been adequately addressed.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#evidence-for-measurement-validity
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#evidence-for-measurement-validity
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Evidence for Measurement Validity
Content validity: does the instrument cover the relevant parts of the construct?
Criterion validity: do scores agree with an appropriate reference or predict a relevant criterion? The quality of the reference matters.
Construct validity: do scores behave as theory predicts, including relationships with related and different constructs?
Validity concerns a particular interpretation and use of scores. Evidence from one population may not establish validity for another.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#example-a-student-stress-questionnaire
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#example-a-student-stress-questionnaire
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Example: A Student Stress Questionnaire



Evidence
Main Validity Concept




Experts check coverage of relevant sources of stress
Content validity


Scores agree with an appropriate reference assessment
Criterion validity


Scores relate to overwhelm as theory predicts
Construct validity



Stress has no simple known reference like a calibration mass. One correlation with another questionnaire is only part of the evidence.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#generalizability
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#generalizability
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Generalizability
A study recruits volunteers from one university’s competitive athletics program.
Its measurements could be consistent and accurate, yet its findings may not apply to all college students or to older adults.
Consider who participated, who did not, the setting, and the conditions of measurement.
A larger sample from the same narrow group does not automatically make the findings broadly generalizable.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-which-validity-concern
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#question-which-validity-concern
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Question: Which Validity Concern?
A researcher asks whether a finding from university athletes applies to adults living in rural communities. Which concern is this?
A. Internal consistency
B. Intra-rater reliability
C. External validity
D. Parallel-forms reliability

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answer-external-validity
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#answer-external-validity
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Answer: External Validity
C. External validity concerns generalizability.
The question asks whether findings apply beyond the study’s participants and setting.
Good measurement helps, but it does not resolve differences in age, health, activity, or environment between these populations.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#excel-practice-a-calibration-readings
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#excel-practice-a-calibration-readings
title: Reliability and Validity

Excel Practice A: Calibration Readings

Calculate differences between readings and between each reading and its reference in G6:I11.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#practice-a-what-the-results-mean
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#practice-a-what-the-results-mean
title: Reliability and Validity
section: Practice A: What the Results Mean
text:
Practice A: What the Results Mean

Mean difference between repeated readings: 0 kg.
Mean difference from the reference, for either reading: +5 kg.
Correlation between reference and Reading 1: r = 1.000.

The repeated readings agree perfectly, but the scale is consistently 5 kg high.
Correlation measures linear association. It does not establish agreement or accuracy. The paired differences reveal the systematic error.

text:
Categorical Refresher: A One-Week Cohort
Now use a separate set of 20 fictional students. All begin without fatigue and complete one week of follow-up.

Short sleep: usual sleep below 7 hours per night.
Not short: usual sleep of at least 7 hours per night.
Outcome: a reported new fatigue episode during follow-up.

This teaching example uses a defined follow-up period so we can calculate risks. It makes no claim about real students or a clinical sleep threshold.


Budget about 15 minutes for the categorical refresher, including Excel Practice B and the following answer slides.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#odds-ratio-refresher
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#odds-ratio-refresher
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Odds Ratio Refresher
Odds compare those with the outcome with those without it.

Short-sleep odds: 6 / 4 = 1.5.
Other-group odds: 2 / 8 = 0.25.
Odds ratio: 1.5 / 0.25 = 6.00.

In G31, use =(G23/H23)/(G24/H24).
Here, OR = 6 and RR = 3. Report the measure you calculated. “Six times the odds” does not mean “six times the risk.”


A conventional case-control sample usually supports an odds ratio; its sample proportions do not directly estimate population risks. This exercise is a cohort with complete follow-up.

objectID: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#interpretation-and-measurement-limits
href: Module 09 - Correlation - Reliability and Validity/Reliability Validity and Application/Reliability Validity and Application.html#interpretation-and-measurement-limits
title: Reliability and Validity
text:
Interpretation and Measurement Limits
The sample shows an association between short sleep and subsequent fatigue. It does not establish causation.

Measurement: did everyone interpret “fatigue” in the same way?
Internal validity: could other differences between the groups explain the association?
External validity: would this volunteer sample represent other students or adults?

This exercise is descriptive. We will address inference later. Do not interpret these calculations as a test of statistical significance.
